surveys.summary: Graphnosis's retrieval is a staged pure pipeline over an in-memory dual graph — decompose → synonym-expand → dual seed pools (TF-IDF + optional embeddings, max-merged) → source-diversified seeds → best-first BFS with score decay → summary down-weight → post-cut structural completion → optional embedding rerank → retirement strip → prompt serialization. Its organizing obsession is that "same graph + same question = same subgraph" must be a real guarantee, which forces a centralized provenance-keyed tie-break, a monotonic-seq heap tie-break, three deliberately separate time inputs (`now` / `retiredAt` / `asOf`), four independently-argued retirement gates with the instant resolved once, and the removal of ambient `process.env` scoring. The engine is deliberately NOT ported to other languages — tie-breaking, hash iteration order and Unicode handling differ across runtimes — so other languages get HTTP/MCP process boundaries plus a `.gai` conformance suite that tests refusals. The single most transferable asset is the commenting discipline: nearly every non-obvious line records the defect it was written to fix and the measurement that decided it.

findings.title: Tie-break on provenance (file, offset, contentHash), never on the surrogate id
findings.whatItIs: One 91-line module centralizes all score-tie ordering. `tieBreakKey` resolves a node to `{file, offset, hash}` from `node.source` + `node.contentHash`; `compareTieKeys` compares those three fields ONE AT A TIME (never a concatenated string key, because no separator provably cannot occur in a file path and a wrong separator silently makes two nodes compare equal). `byScoreThenSource(graph)` returns score-desc-then-provenance and memoizes keys per sort call. Applied at four sites: both seed arms, the merged seed pool, and final node selection.
findings.quote: The obvious fix is to break ties on node id. That is WRONG here, and it was shipped and measured before being caught: ids come from `nanoid()` ... Measured on a 40-question sample: evidence order differed on 21/40 and the evidence SET on 6/40, between two builds inside one single-threaded process.
findings.whyItMatters: The obvious deterministic tie-break — the primary key — is exactly the field that is NOT stable under re-ingest in a system that mints ids per build. They shipped it, measured the damage, and replaced it with the fields that are recomputed identically from the same input. Any retrieval system with generated ids has this bug latent.

findings.title: Unresolvable tie-key returns 0 — arbitrary-but-stable beats random
findings.whatItIs: When the graph is unavailable or the node is missing, `compareTieKeys` returns 0 rather than falling back to id ordering. A stable sort then preserves insertion order — the pre-tie-break behaviour, which reproduced identically run to run. The same reasoning drives passing the retirement gate into the seed finder as a narrow predicate rather than as `graph`, so enabling retirement cannot silently change seed ORDER as a side effect of also enabling provenance tie-breaks.
findings.quote: When no graph is available the comparator returns 0 rather than falling back to id. ... Arbitrary-but-stable beats random.
findings.whyItMatters: Two reusable rules: (a) a degraded comparator should degrade to the previous stable behaviour, not to a different arbitrary one; (b) passing a fat object to enable one capability silently enables every other behaviour keyed on that object — plumb a narrow predicate instead when a change must be measurement-neutral.

findings.title: `asOf`: determinism you must assemble from two fields is not a real property
findings.whatItIs: Three separate temporal inputs: `now` (ranking / expiry damping, default UNSET), `retiredAt` (retirement membership, default WALL CLOCK), `asOf` (supplies the default for both; an explicit `now`/`retiredAt` still wins). Resolution is two lines: `retiredAt = opts.retiredAt ?? opts.asOf ?? Date.now()` and `rankingNow = opts.now ?? opts.asOf`. `{asOf: T}` = graph as it stood at T; `{asOf: T, retiredAt: 0}` = audit view. A bare historical `now` still cannot move retirement.
findings.quote: Determinism you can only get by reading an option list and correctly combining two fields is not a property anyone relies on. `asOf` is that combination, asked for by name.
findings.whyItMatters: The split was forced by a real erasure bug — a caller passing a historical instant for as-of RANKING silently re-admitted content the owner had forgotten after that instant. The second-order lesson is rarer: after splitting, the composite case needed its own name, with asymmetric precedence so the dangerous direction stays closed.

findings.title: "A guarantee a caller must opt into is not a guarantee" — retirement reads the clock
findings.whatItIs: Retirement membership defaults to `Date.now()` even though the headline claim is that retrieval reads no clock. The trade is stated: forgotten content must not reach a prompt whether or not the caller passed an instant. Ranking stays clock-free by default; only membership pays. Wall-clock recency BOOSTS were removed entirely (a x1.3 "accessed in last 24h" bonus made the same file rank differently on Tuesday vs Friday); standing earned by use is scored from `accessCount`, which travels in the serialized file.
findings.quote: Reading the clock here is a deliberate trade against the "retrieval reads no clock" property: a guarantee a caller must opt into is not a guarantee.
findings.whyItMatters: A crisp rule for deciding which safety property gets the default: the one whose failure is unrecoverable. And a clean distinction between standing earned by FILE STATE (reproducible) vs by CLOCK STATE (not) that most memory systems conflate under "recency".

findings.title: Four retirement gates, one resolved instant, and a deliberately-omitted fifth
findings.whatItIs: Retired nodes are excluded at seeding, traversal, structural expansion, and a final `stripRetired` before serialization. The instant is resolved ONCE per query so the gates cannot disagree mid-query. Traversal blocks CONDUCTION not just membership — a retired node cannot relay score between two live nodes it alone connects — and the backward-edge guard exists because `supersedes` runs old→new, so seeding on the new node walks one hop into the fact it replaced. A fifth guard inside final selection was deliberately NOT added because it is unreachable and therefore un-mutation-testable.
findings.quote: Shipping a guard no test can fail buys false confidence, not safety. The one deliberate second layer is `stripRetired` in query-engine, which IS exported and directly tested.
findings.whyItMatters: Defense-in-depth with a testability criterion: a redundant guard is kept only when it can be independently exercised, and `stripRetired` is exported precisely so it can be. Also the conduction insight — filtering the final selection misses the case where a forgotten node is invisible in the prompt yet decisive over its contents.

findings.title: Best-first under a hop budget: the search state is (node, hop), not node
findings.whatItIs: Score strictly decreases per hop (DECAY_FACTOR 0.6 x edge weight in (0,1]), so pops are non-increasing and the first pop of a node is its path maximum — which makes a node-keyed `visited` set look safe. It isn't under a HOP BUDGET: a frontier entry carries score AND remaining hops, so an entry at (0.3, hop 1) is worse on score but can reach a level that (0.5, hop 2) never can. Fix: `expandedAtHop: Map<NodeId, number>` re-expands only at a strictly smaller hop (bounding each node to <= maxHops expansions), plus `bestAtHop: Map<NodeId, number[]>` as the enqueue guard.
findings.quote: Caught by the random differential in tests/unit/traversal-path-maximum.test.ts — 1 disagreement in 200 graphs, which neither the hand-built counterexample nor 400 corpus queries found.
findings.whyItMatters: A genuine, subtle algorithm defect that the textbook Dijkstra-with-visited argument hides, and it only surfaces because of the hop cap every practical graph retriever imposes. The dominance-vs-membership framing ports directly to any budgeted best-first search.

findings.title: Two measured frontier guards: skip hop-limit pushes, key enqueue on (node, hop)
findings.whatItIs: `worthVisiting` returns false immediately when `nextHop >= maxHops`, because such entries are popped and discarded without expanding and their score is already recorded before the call — so skipping the push provably cannot change output. Separately, admitting every entry that arrives with more hop budget is correct but re-queues a node once per incoming edge; keying the guard on (node, hop) drops only states already dominated on BOTH score and budget, bounding the heap at |V| x maxHops.
findings.quote: Measured on a 20,000-node graph: 86% of best-first pushes were these, and dropping them took the traversal from 110 ms to 47 ms. ... Admitting every such entry is correct but ruinous: measured at 3.1x the FIFO query time on an 18,968-node graph.
findings.whyItMatters: Both optimizations ship with the measurement AND the correctness argument for why the skip is output-neutral. That pairing — perf claim plus "here is why this cannot change results" — is what makes an optimization reviewable rather than a leap of faith.

findings.title: A cosine ULP clamp is load-bearing for a traversal proof three modules away
findings.whatItIs: Cosine of identical vectors measures 1.0000000000000002 often enough to matter, and that value becomes an EDGE WEIGHT. Best-first's path-maximum property requires every hop multiplier < 1, so both cosine functions clamp to [-1, 1] at source. The (0,1] premise held only for the ingest path, so `fromSerializable` now REFUSES Infinity, NaN, negative, 0 and `1/DECAY_FACTOR` — while still ACCEPTING 1.0000000000000002, because refusing to open an already-written memory over one ULP would be a data-availability bug introduced in the name of a correctness one.
findings.quote: a 1-ULP overshoot is the difference between an invariant that holds by construction and one that holds by luck. Clamped at the source rather than patched up at every consumer.
findings.whyItMatters: Shows the full chain: identify the invariant an algorithm rests on, find every path into the data that can violate it (five loaders, not one), enforce at the funnel, and calibrate strictness against real already-written data rather than against the ideal.

findings.title: Refusal to port: hash iteration order, tie-breaking and Unicode are the named reasons
findings.whatItIs: One implementation of the engine, on purpose. Other languages get a process boundary — HTTP `serve` on :7777 and an MCP server over the same binary — plus a `.gai` format spec and a conformance suite whose fixtures are half malformed on purpose, because "the useful question about a format reader is not what it accepts but what it REFUSES". Every named hazard is real in the code: the pipeline iterates Map/Set (insertion-ordered by JS spec, randomized in Go) at seed merge, candidate collection, score entries and edge collection; `\b` is replaced with `\p{L}\p{N}\p{M}` lookarounds; analyzers do NFD folding and `toLocaleLowerCase(lang)`.
findings.quote: independent ports are the fastest way to lose that, because tie-breaking, hash iteration order and Unicode handling all differ subtly between runtimes ... So other languages get a process boundary, not a rewrite.
findings.whyItMatters: A defensible, non-parochial answer to "why is this TypeScript-only?" that ships the compensating artifacts (protocol surface + spec + refusal-testing conformance suite) rather than just asserting the position. Also names the one place their determinism does NOT hold: cold ingest with optional LLM summaries.

findings.title: Env vars are ambient state that invalidates golden vectors
findings.whatItIs: `scoreRule` (max-wins vs additive) was readable ONLY from `process.env.GNOSIS_SCORE_RULE`, read at call time inside the traversal. An adopter with that variable set got different rankings from an identical graph and query with nothing in the API to reveal it. Now it is a typed option on both `TraverseOptions` and `QueryOptions`; the env var survives as a deprecated fallback so existing ablation harnesses keep running, but an explicit option always wins.
findings.quote: any published golden vector was valid only alongside an undeclared env state. T4 ("same query, same memory, same answer") cannot hold under those conditions.
findings.whyItMatters: The sharp framing is about EVIDENCE, not just purity: undeclared ambient state does not merely make behaviour vary, it silently invalidates every recorded measurement and regression baseline taken under it.

findings.title: Seeds decide what ENTERS traversal; sourceFloor decides what SURVIVES it
findings.whatItIs: Two distinct diversification knobs, deliberately not wired together. `diversify` (default on) round-robins SEEDS by source file. `sourceFloor` (default OFF) reserves N final subgraph slots per source before score takes the remainder, then re-sorts into score order because "the floor decides membership, not presentation". Wiring the floor to `diversify` was refused because it would change retrieval for every existing caller and the trade is corpus-dependent.
findings.quote: Score alone answers "what is most relevant", which is right for a lookup and wrong for an aggregation ... The answer that comes back is then a correct count of an incomplete set, stated with the confidence of a complete one.
findings.whyItMatters: Names a failure mode most RAG systems never diagnose — top-k relevance produces confidently-wrong counts — and ships BOTH measurements (seed diversification alone left 19/20 final nodes in one source; floor 1 took the deepest source from 7 nodes to 2 and replaced 40% of the subgraph) rather than declaring a winner.

findings.title: Structural nodes conduct but do not occupy budget — unless the query matched them
findings.whatItIs: `document` and `section` nodes carry titles/headings, not answers, but they are what lets a walk cross between parts of a source. Once hierarchy edges resolved, one reachable turn put an entire source two hops away and a 30-node budget measured 18 slots of headings against 12 of content. Fix: drop structural node types before selection, EXCEPT when the node was a seed — because then the heading is genuinely the hit. Section nodes stay indexed on purpose. The same shape appears in `blockedEvidencePrefixes`, which blocks edge propagation but never membership.
findings.quote: they conduct, and they can still be SEEDS when a heading is genuinely what the question matches ... What they no longer do is occupy a slot merely for having been walked through.
findings.whyItMatters: A general, reusable distinction between a node's role as CONDUCTOR and as EVIDENCE, resolved by provenance of arrival (seed vs walked) rather than by type alone. Applies to any hierarchical chunking scheme that indexes headings.

findings.title: Prompt serialization: rank-assigned short ids, weighted typed edges, role-split blocks
findings.whatItIs: The subgraph is rendered as `[n1|type|score|src:...|date:...] content` with short ids assigned in score order (the model never sees a nanoid), then `--- SESSION SUMMARIES ---` (index-level, with a `claims:` sub-line of atomic countable facts split on ' || ', capped at 10), `--- NODES ---` (evidence, structural types filtered out), `--- DIRECTED ---` as `n2 -[causes:0.8]-> n5`, `--- UNDIRECTED ---` as `n2 ~[similar-to:0.4]~ n7`. Edges are emitted only when both endpoints resolved. The system prompt then teaches the model what each edge type means and how to read `date:` tags.
findings.whyItMatters: A concrete, token-efficient encoding for handing an LLM a graph rather than a ranked list: edge WEIGHTS are printed not just edge existence, provenance and date ride inline on every node, and summaries vs raw evidence are separated by epistemic role so the model knows which to count from.

findings.title: Test craft: non-vacuity assertions, random differentials, content-keyed golden vectors
findings.whatItIs: Every guard test also asserts it CAN fail: 'the two orders genuinely DIFFER on this graph', 'the random graphs DO exercise the defect', 'a real built graph produces edges at all — the check is not vacuous'. The path-maximum test runs 2000 mulberry32-seeded random graphs against exhaustive path enumeration, with fixture parameters chosen so the defect can appear (spread weights, a third undirected edges, multiple seeds at different scores so heapify is not trivially ordered). The asOf golden vector is over CONTENT+SCORE not ids, with the `const GOLDEN = got` anti-pattern named in the comment, plus a discrimination check that a different question yields a different vector.
findings.quote: The first draft of this block read `const GOLDEN = got;` — comparing the measurement to itself, which passes unconditionally and proves nothing ... it is easy to write by accident because it looks like a golden vector and prints like one.
findings.whyItMatters: Three reusable disciplines: (1) a guard test must assert its own non-vacuity; (2) a differential against brute force on seeded random inputs finds what hand-built counterexamples and corpus queries both miss; (3) a golden vector's comparison key must be chosen to match the system's own stability guarantee, not its surrogate keys.

antipatterns.title: `compareSeeds` is exported dead code whose 9-line doc contradicts its one-line body
antipatterns.why: The JSDoc explains provenance tie-breaking at length and explicitly warns that the tie-break is NOT on node id; the body is `return b.score - a.score;` — score only, no provenance, no graph. Grep across src/, tests/ and spec/ finds zero call sites. A reader porting seed-finder.ts would reasonably copy this as "the seed comparator" and silently lose the entire tie-break discipline the rest of the repo is built on.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/query/seed-finder.ts:80-94 (doc), :89-94 (body); zero call sites across src/, tests/, spec/

antipatterns.title: The serializer's own sort is not tie-broken — the one module whose output reaches the model
antipatterns.why: `serializeSubgraph` sorts nodes by `scoreB - scoreA` alone. It preserves upstream ordering only because ES2019 `Array.prototype.sort` is stable and the input arrives pre-tie-broken. That is an implicit, untested contract in exactly the module the tie-break doc blames for the original leak ('the subgraph serializer sorts by score alone — so the reordering lands in the prompt verbatim'). Any future caller handing it an un-tie-broken list reopens the bug with no test failing.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/query/subgraph-serializer.ts:18-22; src/core/query/tie-break.ts:15-17

antipatterns.title: Per-query cost is O(V + E) regardless of result size — no cached graph-side derived state
antipatterns.why: `traverseGraph` rebuilds three full adjacency maps over every edge on every call; `collectSupersededIds` scans all directed edges per query; `expandWithStructuralContext` iterates every node in the graph and re-sorts every file's chunk list; final edge collection scans all edges again. The TF-IDF side has a generation-invalidated `DerivedIndex` (WeakMap) and the synonym map is memoized on a mutation signature — the graph side got neither, so the two halves of the same read path have opposite caching disciplines.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/query/traverser.ts:213-233, :547, :555; src/core/graph/retirement.ts:216-222 called at src/core/query/query-engine.ts:238; src/core/query/query-engine.ts:584-612; contrast src/core/similarity/tfidf.ts:253-285 and src/core/query/synonym-expander.ts:19-33

antipatterns.title: `process.env.GNOSIS_SCORE_RULE` is still a live fallback on the default path
antipatterns.why: The module's own doc calls this env var the reason 'T4 cannot hold' and says 'any published golden vector was valid only alongside an undeclared env state' — then keeps it reachable for any caller who does not pass an explicit `scoreRule`, which is the default. Deprecated-but-live ambient state inside the function whose purity is the headline product claim; a stray export in a CI shell silently changes ranking.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/query/traverser.ts:16-28 (the indictment), src/core/query/traverser.ts:208-210 (the live fallback)

antipatterns.title: The router is hand-tuned English regexes calibrated to one benchmark's question mix
antipatterns.why: Five multi-hundred-character alternations whose ORDER is load-bearing and untested, explicitly 'Calibrated against the actual LongMemEval_s question distribution', including literals like `valentine'?s day` and `new year'?s`. It is monolingual while `query-decomposer.ts` and the analyzer stack are carefully multilingual — an inconsistency inside one pipeline. Steal the architecture (classify -> retrieval dials + prompt block, with `source` recorded and ground-truth off by default); do not steal the patterns.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/query/router.ts:45-95, :97-107; contrast src/core/query/query-decomposer.ts:29-49 (9-language splitting)

antipatterns.title: The aggregation prompt block exists twice verbatim with no test asserting they match
antipatterns.why: The multi-session counting directive is duplicated between the legacy inline path in `buildGraphPrompt` and `router.buildCategoryPromptBlock`. It is kept deliberately for A/B parity against a prior measurement run, but it is a ~10-line copy-paste that will drift, and nothing compares the two strings. A one-word edit to one copy silently makes the router and legacy arms non-comparable — the exact property the duplication exists to preserve.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/query/query-engine.ts:861-874; src/core/query/router.ts:176-187

surveys.summary: Graphnosis's data model is deliberately tiny — one `GraphNode` interface, two edge interfaces, three closed string-literal vocabularies (20 node types, 15 directed, 7 undirected) — and both edge layers hang off one shared `Map<NodeId, GraphNode>` and are relaxed in a single traversal pass, the only asymmetry being a ×0.5 penalty for following a directed edge backwards. Essentially all the intellectual content lives not in the types but in the semantics welded onto three or four scalar fields (`validUntil`, `confidence`, `contentHash`, `metadata.retiredBy`) and in ~800 lines of load-bearing comments that each record a shipped defect, the corpus and numbers it was measured on, the rejected alternative, and the residual cost accepted. The strongest material is the mutation semantics: retirement vs content-expiry disambiguated by an administrative marker rather than by the timestamp alone; retirement *reason* (`delete` vs `supersede`) as the key deciding whether re-ingesting an unchanged source file may resurrect content; indelible edits (edit == supersede, old node retired and still readable, `supersedes` edge old→new); and a determinism discipline ("T4") that repeatedly refuses convenient designs — id-based tie-breaking, wall-clock recency boosts, env-var scoring, telemetry writes during retrieval — because they make the same file plus the same query return different answers. The weak spots are the persistence layer (module-global singletons, full delete-and-reinsert saves, no FKs on edge endpoints) and a few edge-construction paths (uncapped co-occurrence edges, quadratic `defines` substring matching) that contradict the repo's own published bounds.

findings.title: Both edge layers relaxed in one frontier pop; backward directed hops damped x0.5
findings.whatItIs: `traverseGraph` builds three adjacency maps over the same node set — `outEdges`, `inEdges`, `undirectedAdj` — and on every frontier pop relaxes all three into one shared `nodeScores` map. Score propagation is identical for outgoing directed and undirected edges (`decayedScore * edge.weight`); following a directed edge backwards costs an extra ×0.5. So the association layer is never a fallback or a second query — the two layers are one walk over one node set, and edge `weight` is uniformly a multiplier on propagated score. SPEC.md turns this into a conformance expectation for any reader claiming 'dual-graph retrieval'.
findings.quote: walk **both** edge layers in one pass rather than treating undirected edges as a fallback
findings.whyItMatters: The cheap version of a 'dual graph' is two indexes queried separately and merged; that produces two ranked lists, not one neighbourhood a walk can cross. Doing it as one frontier with a per-layer multiplier is what makes typed-logic and association evidence compete against each other under one budget, and the backward-hop damping is the minimum honest concession that a directed edge asserts something asymmetric.

findings.title: validUntil carries two facts; an administrative marker splits retired from expired
findings.whatItIs: One optional timestamp encodes four states: unset = live; future = live (temporal fact not yet due); past **with** an administrative retirement marker = retired (invisible to retrieval); past **without** one = expired (content semantics — damped ×0.3 in ranking, still eligible). Three predicates implement it: `isRetired` (administrative ∧ clock), `isExpired` (clock ∧ ¬administrative), `isAdministrativelyRetired` (clock-free, so `retiredAt: 0` works as an audit hatch). The marker test is a four-way OR spanning marker generations: current `metadata.retiredBy`, legacy `deletedAt`, legacy `forgottenAt`, and an outgoing `supersedes` edge that only counts when the node also carries a `validUntil` stamp.
findings.quote: That treated every expired temporal fact as forgotten — "my parking permit expires 30 June" vanished from prompts as though the owner had retracted it.
findings.whyItMatters: Any memory store with time-bounded facts eventually conflates 'this window closed' with 'the owner retracted this', and the conflation is invisible because both look like a past timestamp. The fix — require a separate administrative marker, and make the marker test clock-free so audit/as-of views stay possible — is small and portable, and the `supersedes`-edge clause exposes the trap in the naive version: a caller-supplied edge type from a public union becoming a markerless, clock-free liveness switch.

findings.title: Retirement reason (delete vs supersede) decides whether re-ingest may resurrect content
findings.whatItIs: `RetirementReason = 'delete' | 'supersede'` is recorded on the node and read by a four-line predicate, `blocksReingest`: live nodes block re-ingest (ordinary dedup), supersede-tombs block it (the source file still carries the text the user corrected away, which is exactly why the correction existed), delete-tombs do NOT block it (forgetting a source then re-adding the file restores it — forgetting is not a permanent ban on a string), and expired-but-not-retired nodes block it (expiry is not a retract). Retirement also *hardens*: `applyDelete` stamps its markers only when it actually retired something, while `applySupersede` upgrades `retiredBy` to `'supersede'` unconditionally.
findings.quote: forgotten ('delete') -> does not block … superseded -> DOES block. The user asserted the stored fact was wrong; the file still carrying the old text is exactly why the correction existed.
findings.whyItMatters: This is the central failure mode of every file-synced knowledge store: the user corrects a fact in the graph, the next sync re-reads the unchanged source, and the corrected-away fact returns as a fresh full-confidence node that outranks its own tomb. The previous test keyed on confidence and failed in both directions (superseded nodes fell out of the blocking set; time-decayed live nodes fell into the duplicate set). Encoding intent as a first-class reason, rather than inferring it from a ranking weight, is the whole fix.

findings.title: Confidence is a ranking weight, never liveness; 0 is reserved as the tombstone marker
findings.whatItIs: `RETIRED_CONFIDENCE = 0` while live nodes are floored at `CONFIDENCE_MIN = 0.01`, and the gap is load-bearing: time-decay drives live memories to the same floor a correction used to write, so confidence cannot distinguish 'retired' from 'old'. `setNodeConfidence` therefore refuses 0 on a live node (it would forge the tombstone signal AND suppress the node with no marker, since traversal multiplies path score by confidence), refuses retired nodes (nothing to affect; the write would destroy the audit signal), refuses empty reasons, throws rather than returning an ignorable error object, and returns a receipt whose `applied` is read back from the node after assignment rather than echoed from the argument. The batch form is all-or-nothing and refuses a repeated node id outright.
findings.quote: Content that disappears with no marker is the one outcome the retirement discipline exists to make impossible; a confidence primitive must not provide a side door to it.
findings.whyItMatters: Two transferable rules: (1) a scalar that feeds ranking must not double as a visibility gate, because any decay policy eventually collides with the sentinel values; (2) an audit receipt must be produced by reading state back, not by describing intent — the module documents a real consuming app with a permanent graph-vs-log split caused by logging an increment while the graph received something else.

findings.title: Edge weights validated at the one load funnel, using the proof's bound not the writer's
findings.whatItIs: `fromSerializable` is the single funnel every load path uses (`readGai`, `fromBuffer`, the SQLite loader, the public export), so `assertEdgeWeights` runs there. Writers emit weights in (0, 1], but the check uses `CEILING = 1 / DECAY_FACTOR` (≈1.667) because what the traversal proof actually needs is `DECAY_FACTOR * w < 1`. That tolerates 1-ULP cosine overshoots measured on real round-trips (1.0000000000000002) — refusing to open an existing memory over one ULP would be a data-availability bug introduced in the name of a correctness one — while still refusing Infinity, NaN, ≤0 and anything that would invert score ordering. Failure is a coded error (`GRAPH_EDGE_WEIGHT_INVALID`).
findings.quote: The bound is the PROOF's bound, not the writers' convention.
findings.whyItMatters: Two ideas worth stealing: pick the validation threshold from what downstream correctness actually requires rather than from what your writer happens to emit (maximising compatibility without weakening the guarantee), and put the check at the single choke point every deserializer funnels through. The named failure mode is instructive — an out-of-range weight makes best-first pops stop arriving in non-increasing order, so the dominance test discards strictly better entries and retrieval returns a confidently wrong ranking with no error anywhere.

findings.title: Ranking ties break on content provenance, never on node id
findings.whatItIs: Node ids come from `nanoid()` at build time, so they are not stable across ingests of the same corpus. The tie-break comparator keys on `(source.file, source.offset, contentHash)` — all three persisted and all three recomputed identically from the same input. Fields are compared one at a time rather than concatenated into a composite string key, because no separator provably cannot occur in a file path and a wrong separator silently makes two different nodes compare equal. Unresolvable nodes compare as 0 so a stable sort preserves insertion order ('arbitrary-but-stable beats random'), and keys are memoised per comparator. A richer six-field variant (`file, offset, section, type, hash, chunkOrder`) orders edge-building decisions and is exported for direct testing.
findings.quote: An id tie-break does not make ranking reproducible; it makes it reproducibly arbitrary within a build and freshly arbitrary between builds.
findings.whyItMatters: The measured cost of the naive version is stated: evidence order differed on 21/40 questions and the evidence SET on 6/40, between two builds inside one single-threaded process, and the serializer sorts by score alone so the reordering landed verbatim in the model prompt. The module is 91 dependency-free lines and directly portable. The companion insight — that a comparator unreachable through integration fixtures must be tested directly, and that two prior 'guarding' fixtures were inert, each passing 20/20 against a surgically reverted comparator — is a testing lesson on its own.

findings.title: One canonical non-crypto content hash, plus a rule that every merge verifies content
findings.whatItIs: `content-hash.ts` exists solely to collapse three byte-identical private `simpleHash` copies into one definition, because the invariant `∀n: n.contentHash = h(n.content)` needs a single `h` to be checkable. The hash is DJB2 folded to 32 bits, base36 — ~25% chance of at least one collision at 50k nodes — so both merge sites bucket by hash and then compare exact content: the incremental ingest path and the deduplicator, which hard-deletes the loser. It is deliberately NOT widened, because changing the function changes every `contentHash` in every existing `.gai` file (a format break, not a refactor). The weakness is published in the spec's 'Known weaknesses' section, and the `charCodeAt`/UTF-16-surrogate caveat is documented for anyone comparing against a hash computed elsewhere.
findings.quote: A hash match is a hint, never a proof of identity.
findings.whyItMatters: Content-hash identity is the standard way to key dedup in knowledge stores and the standard way to lose data silently: a collision that merges two different memories reports nothing. The transferable rules are (1) exactly one definition of the hash, because three copies are three chances to drift and drift splits or merges memories depending on which code path wrote the node, and (2) hash equality is a bucketing hint that must be confirmed against content before any destructive action — with the failure direction chosen deliberately ('a redundant node costs space, a destroyed one costs a memory').

findings.title: Re-ingest dedup keys on content+type+file+section, deliberately never chunk order
findings.whatItIs: On append, an incoming chunk matches a stored node when content, type, source file and source section are all equal — positional chunk order is excluded because it indexes the whole document, so inserting one paragraph shifts every chunk below it and order-matching re-stored the entire tail of an edited source as second live copies, compounding on every edit. Multiplicity is preserved instead by a `consumedMatches` set: N identical passages consume N distinct stored nodes, one each, so the Nth occurrence matches the Nth stored node wherever the text moved to. `source.section` IS matched, and the comment records that the first version of the repair omitted it and what broke (occurrence-order pairing let a Beta passage claim a stored Alpha node, giving a later Beta continuation a mislabelled `precedes` predecessor). A separate in-batch collapse keyed on `(file, type, order)` handles the same document handed in twice.
findings.quote: Matching on it made re-appending an EDITED source re-store the entire tail as second active copies — indexed, parented, and served as query seeds — compounding on every subsequent edit.
findings.whyItMatters: Re-syncing an edited file into an append-only store is the central correctness problem of a file-backed memory system, and this is a worked solution with both the failure it fixes and the residual cost it accepts (renaming a heading re-stores that tail under the new heading and leaves the old copy attributed to the old one — 'explicit additive history beats silently mislabelled nodes'). It also names the missing primitive that would eliminate both: a source-replacement operation that retires the previous generation.

findings.title: Cross-generation edges: without them each append is its own connected component
findings.whatItIs: The batch edge builder derives its term index from the chunks handed to it, so on an append it links new nodes to each other and to nothing already stored, however much vocabulary they share; the isolation compounds with every append. `buildCrossGenerationEdges` closes it using the query path's own derived postings index: accumulate shared-IDF mass per already-stored node, skip terms with ≥500 postings, rank by mass with the provenance comparator as tie-break, take 50, then apply the same threshold, same degree cap and same edge type as the in-batch pass. The caller seeds the degree map from every endpoint of every existing undirected edge so the per-node cap is honoured across both passes rather than each pass spending the whole budget.
findings.quote: Retrieval still reaches old and new material, because seeding runs over the corpus-wide lexical index — but it reaches them SEPARATELY, as unrelated results, rather than as one neighbourhood a walk can cross.
findings.whyItMatters: The diagnosis is the valuable part and it generalises to any incrementally-built similarity graph: the bug is invisible to seed-level recall metrics (the lexical index is corpus-wide, so both generations are found) and shows up only in traversal reach, which is exactly the metric nobody instruments. Cost is proportional to the terms the new nodes carry rather than to graph size, and the fix explicitly mirrors the in-batch pass so a rebuild reproduces the same semantic graph despite fresh node ids.

findings.title: Derived-but-persisted structures carry their generating policy id in artifact metadata
findings.whatItIs: `GraphMetadata` carries three provenance ids alongside the counts: `analyzerAdapterId` (how content was tokenized — load fails closed with `AnalyzerMismatchError` on mismatch), `edgePolicyId` (which undirected-candidate policy built the edges), and `ingestPolicyId` (which source-chunk write policy produced the nodes, with a `'mixed'` value when a legacy graph later receives current-policy nodes, plus a per-node `metadata.ingestPolicyId` to distinguish generations). The stated reason for `edgePolicyId` is precise: edges are persisted and never rebuilt on load, so a graph ingested under two policies carries both permanently with no other way to tell. Defaults never change silently — adopting a new policy is an explicit act, a re-ingest.
findings.quote: `analyzerAdapterId` pins how content was tokenized; this pins how it was linked.
findings.whyItMatters: A general rule for any persisted artifact containing derived data: every knob that changed how the derived part was produced must be recorded in the artifact, or the artifact becomes uninterpretable the moment the knob moves. The `'mixed'` value is the honest handling of the case everyone ignores — an artifact that has accumulated content under two generations — and failing closed on analyzer mismatch (a corpus tokenised under one stopword set and queried under another has an index that disagrees with its own contents) is the right default.

findings.title: Orphan hard-deletion removed from the build path: pruning removes edges, never nodes
findings.whatItIs: `buildGraph` runs auto-pruning only above 50 nodes and passes `removeOrphans: false`. Previously true, it hard-deleted every node left with no edges — no owner action, no tombstone, no op-log entry, and no way to tell afterwards — measured on the LongMemEval corpus as silently discarding 80 of 3,747 nodes at one scale and 467 of 19,416 at another (2.1% / 2.4%). Edge pruning is retained at `minDirectedWeight 0.05` / `minUndirectedWeight 0.1` and removed 0 edges on that corpus. Callers who genuinely want the hard delete must ask for it explicitly.
findings.quote: An unconnected node is still a memory. It simply has no neighbours yet — and on the incremental path a later ingest may well give it some. Deleting it is a retrieval-tuning decision destroying user content.
findings.whyItMatters: The generalisable point is the boundary it draws: a retrieval-quality heuristic may reduce prominence but may never destroy stored content, and 'has no edges' is a statement about the current graph, not about the value of the memory — especially in a store whose ingest is incremental. The measurement is the argument; without the 2.1%/2.4% numbers this reads as a taste call.

findings.title: Four retirement gates on one resolved instant, plus a ruling on which guards ship
findings.whatItIs: Retired content is excluded at seeding, at traversal (scoring, conduction, and both edge directions), at structural completion, and by a final `stripRetired` before serialization. `retiredAt` and `supersededIds` are each resolved exactly ONCE per query so the gates cannot disagree mid-query. Two opposite rulings govern the redundancy: a retirement filter at the traverser's final selection was DELETED because every path into the score map is already gated, making it unreachable and un-mutation-testable ('deleting it was caught 0 times in 10 runs'); `stripRetired` was KEPT despite being equally unreachable, because it is exported and directly tested and sits at the last point before content becomes a prompt string, so every future stage inserted between traversal and serialization gets audited by it for free.
findings.quote: Shipping a guard no test can fail buys false confidence, not safety.
findings.whyItMatters: Both halves transfer. 'Resolve the policy instant once per operation so independent gates cannot disagree' names a real bug class — a node live for seeding and retired for serialization is how a tombstone claims a slot no live node can use. And the paired rulings give a usable criterion for defense-in-depth: keep the redundant guard exactly where it is directly testable and sits on a boundary future code will cross; delete it where it is unreachable and therefore unfalsifiable.

findings.title: Three named time inputs: now (ranking), retiredAt (membership), asOf (both)
findings.whatItIs: `now` controls only expiry damping and telemetry stamps and is unset by default, so ranking is a pure function of (graph, question). `retiredAt` controls retirement membership and defaults to the wall clock, explicitly never inheriting from `now` — a caller passing a historical instant for as-of ranking used to silently re-admit content forgotten after that instant. `retiredAt: 0` is the audit hatch that disables the gates. `asOf` was then added as the named combination, because determinism obtainable only by knowing to set two fields to the same value is not a property anyone relies on; it supplies the default for both while an explicit `now`/`retiredAt` still wins, so `{asOf: T, retiredAt: 0}` is the audit view. Separately, wall-clock recency boosts were deleted from ranking while `accessCount`-based standing was kept, because the latter is serialized graph state that travels in the file.
findings.quote: a ×1.3 boost for "accessed within the last 24 hours" makes the same file and the same query rank differently on Tuesday than on Friday
findings.whyItMatters: Most systems have one ambient `now` and inherit it everywhere, which is precisely how an as-of query becomes a privacy regression (a historical ranking instant silently resurrects deleted content). Splitting the clock by what it governs — prominence vs visibility — and defaulting the visibility clock to the wall clock ('a guarantee a caller must opt into is not a guarantee') while defaulting the ranking clock to unset is a clean, portable discipline. The `asOf` convenience field is the right answer to the resulting ergonomics problem.

findings.title: Structural nodes conduct score and can seed, but never occupy a slot merely for being walked
findings.whatItIs: `document` and `section` nodes carry a title or heading, not an assertion — in a conversation ingest those headings are 'turn 3' and 'user 1'. They exist for connectivity (document→section→turn via `contains`), so they must conduct score. Once the hierarchy edges started resolving, a single reachable turn put an entire source two hops away and measured 18 of 30 budget slots going to headings against 12 to content. The rule: `section` nodes ARE indexed on purpose (a '## Deployment checklist' heading is genuine query signal) and are kept when they were seeds, but are dropped before final selection when they were only walked through; `document` nodes are excluded from the index entirely and skipped by the embedding pass. The spec states this is a policy decision, not a format one.
findings.quote: they conduct, and they can still be SEEDS when a heading is genuinely what the question matches … What they no longer do is occupy a slot merely for having been walked through.
findings.whyItMatters: Any hierarchical ingest creates nodes that are structurally necessary and semantically empty, and the two obvious policies are both wrong: exclude them and the graph loses the edges that let a walk cross a document; include them and scaffolding crowds out evidence exactly on the multi-source questions that need breadth most. The resolved position — conduct always, occupy a slot only when directly matched — is the non-obvious third option, and the node-type vocabulary encodes the structural/assertional distinction so the policy is expressible at all.

antipatterns.title: Module-global mutable graph and DB singletons, with a swap hack for multi-instance use
antipatterns.why: `graph-store.ts` keeps the 'current graph' in a module-level `let currentGraph`, and `sqlite-store.ts` keeps a module-level `let db`. `openSqliteStore(dbPath)` exists to give SDK callers a store that does not inherit `process.cwd()` or the singleton — but it is implemented by assigning the module global inside a try/finally around every call. This is non-reentrant: two store handles in one process, or any async interleaving inside a swapped region, silently cross-wire. The correct shape (pass the handle through, or make each store a closure over its own handle) is strictly simpler than the hack.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/graph/graph-store.ts:8-20; src/core/persistence/sqlite-store.ts:34-45; src/core/persistence/sqlite-store.ts:309-330

antipatterns.title: Persistence is delete-everything-then-reinsert per save, with no FK or index on edge endpoints
antipatterns.why: `saveGraph` deletes every node and edge row for the graph and reinserts them all inside one transaction — O(|V|+|E|) per call regardless of how little changed — which defeats the incremental `addDocumentsToGraph` API it exists to persist. The schema declares foreign keys only on `graph_id`; `from_node`, `to_node`, `node_a`, `node_b` have none, and there is no index on undirected endpoints, so the SQL store can hold dangling edges that the `.gai` reader rejects outright (`GAI_DANGLING_EDGE`) — the constraint is only re-imposed at load time via `fromSerializable`. The same file also lazy-loads its native dependency with `eval('require')` to dodge tsc transformation, defeating bundler analysis and any code-generation-restricted runtime.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/persistence/sqlite-store.ts:128-170; src/core/persistence/sqlite-store.ts:76-106; src/core/persistence/sqlite-store.ts:15-32; src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:146-157

antipatterns.title: The documented per-node degree cap is not enforced on co-occurrence edges
antipatterns.why: `MAX_EDGES_PER_NODE = 10` is checked and accounted only in the similarity/entity pass. The second pass, which connects each chunk to the next three in its section at fixed weight 0.4, performs no degree check and never updates `edgeCountPerNode` — so a long section adds edges beyond the cap and the cap's own counters are wrong for any later pass that seeds from them (the incremental path does exactly that). AGENTS.md nonetheless publishes 'Max 10 edges per node: Prevents hub explosion' as a performance bound, so a reader porting the capped-degree claim inherits an uncapped association layer.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/graph/undirected-edges.ts:17-18; src/core/graph/undirected-edges.ts:117-153; src/core/graph/undirected-edges.ts:156-180; src/core/graph/incremental.ts:271-274

antipatterns.title: `defines` edges are quadratic substring matching with regex-guessed subjects and no cap
antipatterns.why: For every chunk typed `definition`, the builder extracts a term with four English-only sentence-prefix regexes and then scans EVERY other chunk with `other.content.toLowerCase().includes(term)`, emitting a `defines` edge at fixed weight 0.6. No word-boundary check, no weight threshold, no degree cap, no posting-list guard — so a definition of a short or common term links to a large fraction of the corpus, and the pass is O(n²) in chunk count while the neighbouring similarity pass goes to real trouble to stay near-linear. The identical substring bug was found and fixed elsewhere in this codebase with a Unicode word-boundary regex (`forgetTopic('aster')` had retired 2,151 nodes, 127 of them only because of 'Pilaster'); the fix was never carried back here.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/graph/directed-edges.ts:50-61; src/core/graph/directed-edges.ts:90-103; src/core/corrections/correction-engine.ts:398-422

antipatterns.title: Liveness and audit semantics live in an untyped, unvalidated `metadata` bag
antipatterns.why: `GraphNode.metadata` is `Record<string, string | number>` and the spec declares it 'free-form', yet it carries the fields that decide whether a node is visible at all (`retiredBy`, `deletedAt`, `forgottenAt`), its lineage (`retiredAt`, `retiredReason`), ingest provenance (`ingestPolicyId`, `chunkOrder`) and the confidence audit trail (`confidenceSetAt/From/To/Reason/Writes`). `isRetired` — the security-relevant predicate — is therefore a sequence of string comparisons and `typeof x === 'number'` tests against values no load path validates, while the declared fields (`confidence`, `validUntil`, edge `weight`) do get typed and, for weights, validated at the door. The asymmetry is backwards: the fields that decide visibility are the ones with no schema.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/types.ts:50-75; src/core/graph/retirement.ts:98-108; src/core/graph/graph-store.ts:57-87; SPEC.md:104-121

antipatterns.title: AGENTS.md contradicts the shipped invariants it is supposed to teach
antipatterns.why: The agent-facing guide states 'Auto-pruning: Orphan nodes (zero edges) are removed after graph construction' (false — `removeOrphans: false` since the measured 2.1–2.4% silent data loss), 'Soft-delete sets validUntil + confidence 0.1' (false — `RETIRED_CONFIDENCE = 0`, and the 0-vs-0.01 gap is load-bearing), and 'Content hash deduplication: Identical content produces identical hashes; duplicates are merged' with none of the collision caveat that the code and SPEC §6 both treat as mandatory. This is the first file an AI agent reads; the code comments and the guide now disagree about the invariants and only the code is tested, so an agent following the guide reasons from three retracted rules.
antipatterns.evidence: AGENTS.md (Graph Integrity / Temporal Safety & Forgetting sections); src/core/graph/graph-builder.ts:131-156; src/core/graph/retirement.ts:127-135; src/core/graph/content-hash.ts:16-26

surveys.territory: product scope discipline, docs craft & positioning
surveys.summary: Graphnosis treats prose as a load-bearing engineering artifact: the README leads with a zero-install ten-second demo before any argument, the ROADMAP is an enumerated export-surface list usable as a set-membership triage test with "build it as a separate package" as the stated default for borderline cases, and SPEC.md is written for a stranger who will implement it (a "why not an existing format" table, a quantified known-weaknesses section, per-layer L1/L2/L3 conformance, and a "one break, once" versioning constraint with three named admissible v3 reasons). The honesty norms are the standout: a benchmark badge that literally reads "re-measuring", a withdrawn headline number replaced by reproducible ablation rows with raw per-question JSONL evidence and a verify script, changelog entries that state what a change COSTS in measured numbers, an "Errata (added after release)" section amending a shipped release note, and a spec that places a MUST on the project's own marketing copy not to imply an unencrypted .gai is safe to hand over. Commit subjects are plain-English claims and bodies are four-move arguments (what was wrong / why the obvious reading is wrong / what it costs / what is deliberately deferred), several of which argue against their own change before making it. Against that, the repo carries a large unmaintained shadow-docs tail — a 694-line orphaned enterprise/security doc three months stale, agent-instruction files asserting behaviour the changelog reversed, and a root transcript teaching the wrong magic bytes — where doc quality correlates almost perfectly with recency of edit rather than care at authoring.

findings.title: README leads with a ten-second, network-free demo and delegates the core claim to a picture
findings.whatItIs: The first content after the badges is one runnable line — `npx -y @nehloo/graphnosis@latest demo` — that opens a 3D graph in the browser with "No install, no API key, no network", immediately followed by the same command pointed at the reader's own files. The README then explains the visual grammar (arrowheads = directed typed logic, plain lines = undirected association) and closes the section with "That is the whole idea, and it is easier to see than to read about." The offline property is a build-time commitment, not a boast: the demo viewer is vendored into dist rather than fetched from a CDN specifically so the first line stays true. The known failure modes of that line (npx inside a clone runs the published release; older versions have no `bin`) are documented at the bottom of the README rather than hidden.
findings.quote: That is the whole idea, and it is easier to see than to read about.
findings.whyItMatters: Most READMEs spend 200 lines arguing for a mental model that a 10-second artifact would install for free. The transferable mechanism is the triple: (1) the first line is executable with zero prerequisites, (2) the second line points it at the reader's own data, (3) the claim prose is bad at is handed to the demo explicitly, and the infrastructure is bent (vendoring) to keep the promise literal.

findings.title: ROADMAP as triage: enumerated in-scope, complement out-of-scope, stated default answer
findings.whatItIs: ROADMAP.md declares its own function in sentence one ("It is the reference for triaging issues and pull requests"). In-scope is thirteen bullets naming actual API symbols (query/queryHybrid/prompt, edit/deleteNode/supersede/correct/forgetByTopic/previewForgetTopic/retired, setConfidence, asOf, GraphnosisError/isCorruption/isVersionSkew/isCallerError, migrateAnalyzer, reflect, EmbeddingAdapter/TextAnalyzer, queryGraphs) — so triage is a set-membership test, not a judgement call. Out-of-scope is defined as the complement in one sentence, with an explicit default: "build it as a separate package that depends on Graphnosis." The default is repeated at the end and softened ("but there are exceptions, and a short conversation is the cheapest way to get to the right answer"), and a three-question proposal template makes question 3 "why you think it belongs in the SDK rather than an adjacent package" — putting the scope argument on the applicant. CONTRIBUTING closes the loop with an incentive: community packages get linked from the README.
findings.quote: The default for borderline cases is "build it as a separate package that depends on Graphnosis."
findings.whyItMatters: The asymmetry is the mechanism: exhaustively enumerating in-scope and defining out-of-scope as its complement is what keeps the document finite and maintainable, and turns scope disputes from taste arguments into list lookups. The softened restatement plus the escape hatch is what stops it reading as a wall and killing contributions.

findings.title: One engine implementation on purpose, justified by determinism mechanics
findings.whatItIs: A README blockquote refuses ports in other languages and gives three specific divergence mechanisms rather than a resourcing excuse: tie-breaking, hash iteration order and Unicode handling all differ subtly between runtimes, and independent ports are the fastest way to lose determinism. It then names its own exception in the same paragraph (cold ingest with optional LLM summaries is not deterministic unless the summaries are pinned), and offers the substitute it recommends — "other languages get a process boundary, not a rewrite" — which the repo actually ships as an HTTP `serve` endpoint plus an MCP server on the same binary. Each named divergence mechanism has a matching bug in this repo's own changelog (nanoid-derived tie-breaks differing across builds; ASCII word boundaries meaning non-Latin queries never matched).
findings.quote: So other languages get a process boundary, not a rewrite.
findings.whyItMatters: This is the rare version of "we only support one language" that is a design position rather than a shrug: the refusal is derived from a product guarantee (determinism), evidenced by the project's own regressions, bounded by a stated exception, and paired with a shipped alternative. It also sets up the per-layer conformance model (gcr-11) that lets them court format implementations while refusing engine ones.

findings.title: A benchmark badge that reads 're-measuring', plus recomputable per-question evidence
findings.whatItIs: The slot where every project puts its best number instead says `LongMemEval-re--measuring` in grey. The README's Benchmark section opens "A current headline figure is deliberately not quoted here" because retirement, expiry and structural ranking all moved on this release line, so the last measured score no longer describes installable code. What remains is labelled "historical single-run best" and "a single run each on an older line — read them as evidence that the ablations separate, not as a current score". Underneath: eight raw per-question .jsonl scoring records with checksums.txt and manifest.json; `node benchmarks/evidence/verify.mjs` recomputes each count and exits non-zero on disagreement; the evidence README gives a one-liner a skeptic can run with none of their code (`grep -c '"correct":true' cloud-paired-78.0.jsonl` → 390), explains what sanitization removed and why, and even documents a CLI footgun in the reproduction command. Null and mislabelled runs are annotated in place rather than deleted ("Runs r38-r40 in the benchmark record remain replicates; they are not retro-labelled").
findings.quote: The number returns when the run does.
findings.whyItMatters: Withdrawing your own headline metric because the code changed underneath it, and encoding the withdrawal in the badge itself, is close to unheard of. The mechanism that makes it survivable is that the evidence layer is separable from the claim layer: raw artifacts + a recompute script + a grep one-liner mean the retraction costs the claim, not the credibility.

findings.title: Changelog entries price each change in measured numbers
findings.whatItIs: Fixes are priced. The best-first frontier change is justified against the paper's path-maximum theorem with a concrete counterexample (0.0216 where the theorem requires 0.216) and then priced: "Cost: roughly 1.4x the traversal time of the old order on a 19k-node graph." The v0.10.0 header quantifies caller impact (~9% of queries re-rank, 6% return a different evidence SET) and ships `traversalOrder: 'fifo'` so third parties can re-derive numbers this release invalidated. An earlier "about 41% mean query latency" claim is withdrawn as a constant — with the reason (it cited an unreachable /tmp path and described one point on a curve as an overhead) — replaced by a five-row measured table, and then placed back on that curve: "it is not 'well above' the curve — it is on it." Other entries carry 80/3,747 and 467/19,416 silently-deleted nodes, 127/2,151 unintended retirements, 21-of-40 → 0-of-40 evidence-order instability, and 95 of 211 false person identities extracted from this repo's own markdown.
findings.quote: Cost: roughly 1.4x the traversal time of the old order on a 19k-node graph.
findings.whyItMatters: A changelog that only lists wins is a marketing document. Pricing each change, quantifying blast radius on callers, shipping a compatibility switch so old measurements stay re-derivable, and correcting a withdrawn figure without exaggerating the correction are four separable habits any team can adopt. The null-result entry (an experiment reported as a null, with 'what the number is' separated from 'what the number is evidence for') is the rarest of them.

findings.title: An 'Errata (added after release)' section amending a shipped changelog entry
findings.whatItIs: Under `## v0.10.0`, after the release shipped, a new subsection admits the entry omitted two newly-introduced error message strings, and says so in those words: "Recorded here rather than quietly fixed." Each string then gets its downstream consequence named, and the two consequences are deliberately distinguished — one prefix change causes a load failure to fall through a recovery path, the other causes a consumer to quarantine a perfectly valid file written by a newer version ("Version skew is not corruption and must not be handled as it"). The entry closes with a commitment: the strings are now frozen because they are load-bearing for at least one downstream classifier, and stable codes are planned for 0.11.0. That commitment is then delivered, and the follow-up keeps the messages byte-identical and test-frozen so existing substring classifiers keep working during migration.
findings.quote: 0.10.0 introduced two new error message strings and this entry did not say so. … Recorded here rather than quietly fixed.
findings.whyItMatters: Changelogs are treated as append-only historical records nobody revisits. Treating a past entry as amendable — with an explicit errata marker, the downstream consequence of each omission, and a versioned remediation commitment that is honoured while freezing the accidental contract — is a mechanism for keeping a changelog trustworthy after it has been wrong.

findings.title: Breaking-change classification by which view of a type breaks, plus a both-versions snippet
findings.whatItIs: The v0.11.0 release header enumerates, before any section, the three ways a caller can break even though no public export was removed or renamed: non-unit-norm embedding adapters see seed scores move; TypeScript code that CONSTRUCTS a `CorrectionResult` stops compiling; `err.name === 'Error'` checks now return false — while explicitly stating that message-substring classifiers are unaffected because those strings are frozen and tested. The reasoning is made explicit for the required-field case: it is filed under Changed, not Added, because "'additive' describes the reader's view only, and the constructor's view is the one that breaks a build." Paired with it is a snippet that is correct on both the old and new version (`res.affectedNodeIds?.[0] ?? nodeId`), so a consumer can land the change before upgrading — and a note telling readers which of their own workaround code to delete.
findings.quote: "additive" describes the reader's view only, and the constructor's view is the one that breaks a build.
findings.whyItMatters: Semver has no vocabulary for the producer/consumer asymmetry of structural typing: adding a required field is additive to readers and breaking to anyone who builds the value (mocks, test doubles, wrappers). Naming that axis in the release header, and shipping a both-versions-correct adoption snippet plus a delete-this-workaround note, is a directly portable migration-note format.

findings.title: State the disclaimer where the belief forms, and make it normative on your own docs
findings.whatItIs: The README and the SPEC both say plainly that a .gai body is not encrypted ('strings on one prints them'), and the SPEC diagnoses why the omission was dangerous: the section is titled Integrity and is mostly about HMAC, so a reader scanning for 'is this protected' finds cryptography and stops. It then states the omission is deliberate rather than pending (encryption belongs to the layer that knows the trust boundary — which keys exist, who holds them, how they rotate) and converts the disclaimer into RFC-2119 obligations on the caller, including one placed on the project's own documentation: implementations MUST encrypt across a trust boundary, MUST NOT present a checksum or valid MAC as evidence of confidentiality, and documentation describing .gai portability MUST NOT imply a file is safe to hand over merely because it is self-contained. A follow-on commit applies the same lens to the error taxonomy, correcting `corruption` from 'damaged or forged' because describing it as forgery detection in the doc consumers read while writing their handler is how a downstream system treats an unsigned file as verified.
findings.quote: Documentation and interfaces describing `.gai` portability MUST NOT imply that a `.gai` is safe to hand over merely because it is self-contained.
findings.whyItMatters: The generalized rule is 'audit the document where the reader forms the belief, not the document where the fact is technically true' — and then make that rule normative so it survives the next doc revision. Writing a MUST-NOT against your own marketing copy inside the spec is an unusual and effective way to bind future positioning.

findings.title: NOTICE documents inlined transitive deps of a vendored bundle, and why it is vendored
findings.whatItIs: The NOTICE third-party section names the redistributed bundle and version (3d-force-graph v1.80.0), its copyright holder and licence, then enumerates the dependencies bundled inside the minified file — three.js, three-forcegraph, three-render-objects, d3-force-3d, kapsule, accessor-fn — which a node_modules-walking licence checker would miss entirely because they are inlined into one vendored .min.js. It states where the upstream licence text ships in the published artifact (dist/cli/vendor/3d-force-graph.LICENSE) and, unusually, why the vendoring exists at all: so `npx @nehloo/graphnosis demo` works with no network access. The attribution was itself missing until a later commit that also caught sixteen orphaned files from a removed module surviving every build, including .d.ts declarations for code with no runtime behind it.
findings.quote: The demo viewer vendors it rather than loading it from a CDN, so that `npx @nehloo/graphnosis demo` works with no network access.
findings.whyItMatters: Two transferable details: enumerating the transitive deps that are inlined into a vendored bundle (the case automated licence tooling silently misses), and tying the legal obligation back to the product property that motivated the vendoring, so a future maintainer who considers un-vendoring knows what breaks.

findings.title: Commit subjects are claims, bodies are four-move arguments with explicit Deferred sections
findings.whatItIs: Subjects assert something in English with no ticket refs — "the lockfile records the version it is a lock for", "the corruption class does not mean tampered with", "write section 8 for an implementer, not for a reader of this repo", "match milestone reports by shape, not by name". Bodies follow a repeatable shape: what was actually wrong in mechanism; why the obvious reading of it is wrong; what it costs or explicitly does not change; what is deliberately left undone. The lockfile commit argues against its own change first (the mismatch is three releases old, `npm ci` never checks the root version, it has never broken a release) before landing on the second-order reason. One docs commit ends with a labelled "Deferred:" paragraph naming the two remaining unpinned --help strings and why they belong in a code change, plus a "Worth checking after this lands" note that the new screenshots use repo-relative paths so they render on GitHub but not npmjs.com. Another states its verification method: "Each corrected snippet was executed from a packed tarball in a clean consumer rather than read."
findings.quote: a checklist that has learned to ignore one of its own signals is worth less than one line of diff.
findings.whyItMatters: The four-move body plus a labelled Deferred paragraph is a format that captures the two things normally lost to a reviewer's head — the counter-argument that was considered and rejected, and the known-remaining work with its reason for exclusion. Documenting the verification method (executed from a packed tarball, not read) inside the commit is what makes a docs-correctness claim auditable.

findings.title: A spec written for a stranger who will implement it: per-layer L1/L2/L3 conformance
findings.whatItIs: SPEC.md opens by stating that where spec and implementation disagree the spec is wrong and should be fixed, because "a format with one implementation and no written spec is a file layout, not a standard." §0 rejects five alternative formats each for a specific disqualifying property (Protobuf requires every consumer to compile from the same schema; MessagePack was chosen precisely so no schema coordination is needed). §6 'Known weaknesses' is quantified — the 32-bit contentHash puts a birthday-bound collision at ~5% by 20,000 nodes and 25% by 50,000, with a MUST NOT treat equal hash as equal content — and that exact weakness later bites them in their own dedup path. §8.3 splits conformance into L1 container / L2 model / L3 retrieval+authority on the grounds that a file format benefits from many independent implementations while a retrieval engine does not, and states that declaring L2 is a complete claim rather than a partial one. A commit codifies the editorial rule: passages justifying a requirement by describing this project rather than the format were rewritten, because 'a spec that quotes the contradiction makes it permanent'.
findings.quote: A file format benefits from many independent implementations: that is what proves the bytes are unambiguous. A retrieval engine does not — ranking is a design position, and two engines that rank differently are not two implementations of one thing.
findings.whyItMatters: Per-layer conformance is the cleanest resolution I have seen to the tension between wanting adopters of your format and not wanting forks of your engine: it lets a second implementation make a complete, non-embarrassing claim (L2) without promising to reproduce your ranking. The quantified-weaknesses section and the 'write it for the implementer, not for a reader of this repo' rule are directly portable to any internal spec or RFC.

findings.title: 'One break, once': budget the breakage, name the v3 exceptions, list what v2 refuses
findings.whatItIs: The v2 proposal is governed by a stated constraint: "A format that breaks twice has taught the market that it breaks", so v2 is intended to be the only breaking version and the correct posture is to be greedy now and conservative afterwards. Two enforced consequences: everything in the section lands together or not at all ("A partial v2 is two breaks wearing one version number"), and after v2 extension happens via a `requires[]` must-understand feature-tag list in the header — a reader refuses on an unknown feature tag, never on an unknown version — citing PNG and Matroska, and making the version number "vestigial by design". Three admissible reasons for a v3 are named in advance "because 'never' is not credible". A companion §8.6 lists two things the author wants and is refusing: widening contentHash to SHA-256 (deferred to v3 with a reason the urgency dropped) and a merge algebra ('is not claimed here'). The same discipline appears inside features: (id, rev) gives merge a place to put a conflict and explicitly does not define the merge algebra.
findings.quote: A partial v2 is two breaks wearing one version number.
findings.whyItMatters: This is a budget for breakage rather than a policy against it: it forces every desired break into one release, pre-commits to a non-versioned extension mechanism afterwards, and pre-names the escape hatches so the commitment is credible. The 'Deliberately NOT in v2' list plus the recurring phrase 'is not claimed here' does scope-discipline work inside the design document, which is where scope creep actually originates.

findings.title: Prove the packaged artifact, and prove the prover with a positive control
findings.whatItIs: A verify-package script opens with an essay explaining that all 24 test suites import through the `@/*` alias into src/, so "the artifact consumers actually install is verified by nothing at all", and enumerates four failure modes that ship green today (unrewritten alias specifiers, a runtime file missing from files[], an exports subpath pointing at nothing, a bin with no shebang) — all invisible to tsc, eslint and src-importing tests. It refuses to pack when dist/ is missing, npm packs, installs the tarball into a scratch dir as a real dependency, imports every declared exports subpath from outside the repo, and asserts the root entry exports ≥20 symbols ("A dist that resolves but exports nothing is the subtle version of broken"). Two details stand out: a comment preserving the false failure the check itself caused (grep -rl exits 1 when it finds nothing, and treating non-zero as error inverts the check), and a canary positive control that plants an unrewritten specifier, confirms the grep finds it, then deletes it. The format conformance runner applies the same inversion: half the fixtures are malformed on purpose because 'the useful question about a format reader is not what it accepts but what it REFUSES', and it imports from dist/ so it is the only gate exercising the shipped reader.
findings.quote: a guard reported without its mutation is unproven.
findings.whyItMatters: Two separable, directly portable ideas: (1) a CI step that installs your own published tarball into a clean consumer and imports every declared entry point, catching the entire class of packaging defects that source-importing tests cannot see; (2) mutation-testing the guard itself with an inline positive control, so a check that has never fired is not mistaken for a check that works.

findings.title: CI gates are incident post-mortems, ordered by irreversibility
findings.whatItIs: Every workflow step's comment answers 'why does this exist' with a named past failure. The CI workflow's header explains that nothing ran on push or PR, so the first verification of any change was the tag push inside the publishing job — and names the evidence: tag v0.7.1 sits on origin with no CHANGELOG section, no npm version and no release. The publish workflow extracts the release body from the CHANGELOG and fails if the section is empty, because v0.5.0 shipped to npm with no release notes and was backfilled by hand. The tag-vs-package.json gate is placed last among the checks and immediately before npm publish, explicitly so it also catches anything earlier in the job that rewrote the manifest, since the registry is not retractable. A redundant build step is kept because 'if `prepare` ever stops running it, silence would look like success', and a warning-only step compares package.json to npm latest on main so a duplicate-version failure surfaces before tag time.
findings.quote: A version number was spent to discover a problem this workflow would have caught for free.
findings.whyItMatters: Two portable rules: comment every gate with the specific incident that motivated it (so nobody deletes it as ceremony), and order gates by irreversibility — the check that guards the unretractable step runs last, after everything that could invalidate it. The 'silence would look like success' justification for a redundant step is a good general test for whether a redundancy is waste.

antipatterns.title: A 694-line orphaned enterprise/security doc, three months stale, pointed at from the SDK source
antipatterns.why: enterprise/enterprise.md was last touched 2026-05-09 while README/ROADMAP were revised 2026-08-04. It is the second-longest document in the repo, is linked from no top-level page — but IS linked from src/sdk/index.ts:33 ('See enterprise/enterprise.md for the full IT/security posture'), giving it false authority with exactly the audience it will mislead. It says the codebase is MIT-licensed (it is Apache-2.0), says publishConfig.access is 'restricted' and the package is not on the public registry (package.json:35 says 'public'), uses the pre-0.3.0 .aikg extension ~25 times, and its worked enterprise examples call g.saveAikg / g.loadAikg, methods that do not exist (the shipped names are saveGai/loadGai). A security reviewer following its adoption checklist writes non-compiling code and forms a false belief about the licence. Lesson: a long, high-authority document that no top-level page links to will not be maintained, and the danger scales with how authoritative it sounds — link it or date-stamp it.
antipatterns.evidence: enterprise/enterprise.md:301 (MIT claim); enterprise/enterprise.md:529-531 (restricted access) vs package.json:35 ('access':'public'); enterprise/enterprise.md:579,599,612 (g.loadAikg/g.saveAikg) vs src/sdk/index.ts:951,982 (saveGai/loadGai); src/sdk/index.ts:33 (source points at the stale doc); enterprise/enterprise.md:536 ('Publish with 2FA + OTP') vs .github/workflows/publish.yml:12-16 (npm OIDC, no token)

antipatterns.title: AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md are shadow specs asserting behaviour the changelog later classified as bugs
antipatterns.why: AGENTS.md (last touched 2026-05-09) lists as 'Security and Robustness Guardrails' three behaviours that were subsequently reversed: 'Auto-pruning: orphan nodes are removed after graph construction' — reclassified in v0.8.0 as silent data loss (80/3,747 and 467/19,416 nodes destroyed) and turned off by default; 'Soft-delete sets validUntil + confidence 0.1' — v0.9.0 moved retired nodes to confidence 0 and made 0.1 the LIVE floor, the opposite meaning; 'Confidence decays ~1%/day after 7 days without access' — v0.9.0 found decay was measuring age not disuse and made it opt-in, default off. AGENTS.md:70 also asserts 'All dependencies MIT or Apache-2.0 licensed' with no gate behind it in ci.yml. CLAUDE.md still uses .aikg throughout. Agent-instruction files are documentation with a higher blast radius than prose docs and no reader who will notice they are wrong.
antipatterns.evidence: AGENTS.md:40 vs CHANGELOG.md:765-774; AGENTS.md:43 vs CHANGELOG.md:456-458 and CHANGELOG.md:136-144; AGENTS.md:55 vs CHANGELOG.md:573-584; AGENTS.md:70; CLAUDE.md:56,68,130,146

antipatterns.title: GRAPHNOSIS.md calls the store 'encrypted' — the exact claim two other files were amended to refute
antipatterns.why: GRAPHNOSIS.md:5 says Graphnosis is 'a local, encrypted store the user owns'. SPEC.md:210 says 'The body is not encrypted. A .gai file is readable by anyone who has it.' and README.md:156 says the same. Worse, the encrypted claim violates the normative rule those very edits introduced at SPEC.md:232-235 — documentation describing .gai portability MUST NOT imply a file is safe to hand over merely because it is self-contained. The safety-critical statement was fixed in two files and missed in a third in the same repository. If you make a claim normative, grep for its negation across every tracked file, including the ones you think target a different audience.
antipatterns.evidence: GRAPHNOSIS.md:5 vs SPEC.md:208-212, SPEC.md:232-235, README.md:156-162

antipatterns.title: The 're-measuring' badge links to a document whose first sentence asserts the withdrawn number
