antipatterns.why: README.md:13 points the LongMemEval 're--measuring' badge at benchmarks/benchmarks.md, whose very first content line (benchmarks/benchmarks.md:3) reads, in the present tense, '…a system whose … memory stack … scores 78.00% on the official LongMemEval benchmark, above Zep (71.20%)…', repeated as a section heading at :14. The withdrawal notice does exist — 'No run in this log is current… Every figure below therefore describes code that is no longer the code' — but it is at :402-408, roughly 400 lines below the claim it retracts. So the honest disclaimer is placed under the assertion it withdraws, reached via a link whose anchor text is the retraction. The fix is a lede edit; the correct pattern is already written one file away at README.md:415-423. Retractions must be placed where the reader arrives, not where the narrative reaches them.
antipatterns.evidence: README.md:13; benchmarks/benchmarks.md:3; benchmarks/benchmarks.md:14; benchmarks/benchmarks.md:402-408; README.md:415-423

antipatterns.title: `npm test` is a hand-maintained 25-command && chain with an undeclared build dependency
antipatterns.why: package.json:61 chains 25 `tsx tests/unit/*.test.ts` invocations plus an ablation script and `node spec/conformance.mjs` into one && string with no test runner. Consequences: no parallelism; the first failure hides every later suite; a new test file runs only if someone remembers to append it to the string, so under-coverage is silent rather than a red build; and spec/conformance.mjs:22 imports from dist/, giving `npm test` an undeclared dependency on a prior build:lib. This is the same failure class the repo diagnosed and fixed elsewhere — commit 0c9e833 replaced nine literal filenames in .gitignore with shape-matching globs precisely because 'each new review round shipped untracked only if someone remembered to add it'. The lesson was applied to .gitignore and not to the test script.
antipatterns.evidence: package.json:61; spec/conformance.mjs:22; .github/workflows/ci.yml:48-52

antipatterns.title: original-discussion.md sits at the repo root teaching the wrong magic bytes — the error another doc was deleted for
antipatterns.why: original-discussion.md (415 lines, last touched 2026-05-09) is a verbatim chat transcript plus a Next.js file tree and phase plan that no longer describes the code. Its line 211 documents the format header as '[4-byte magic: 0x47 0x41 0x49 0x01] // "GAI" + version'. The real magic is 0x41 0x49 0x4B 0x47 = 'AIKG' (SPEC.md:245, spec/conformance.mjs:65). Commit 0441884 deleted gai-format/gai-format.md specifically because it carried that identical wrong claim, reasoning that 'an implementation written from that document produces a file the reference reader rejects at byte 0' and that it 'could only be found by someone browsing the repository, which is exactly who would then implement from it'. The removal commit's own justification applies verbatim to the file that survived at the repository root. A document deletion not accompanied by a repo-wide grep for the same false claim is half a fix.
antipatterns.evidence: original-discussion.md:211; SPEC.md:245; spec/conformance.mjs:65; original-discussion.md:257-353 (obsolete Next.js file tree)

surveys.summary: `.gai` is a small, honestly-specified container: 4-byte magic `AIKG`, u32BE headerLen, msgpack header, msgpack body, u32BE additive checksum, optional 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 trailer. The interesting content is not the bytes but the surrounding discipline: a normative spec that names its own weaknesses, a shipped fixture set that is 60% deliberately-malformed files so a second implementation can be held to the same refusals, an error taxonomy keyed on what a consumer should DO (corruption vs version-skew vs caller) rather than on what went wrong, frozen message strings guarded by a source-scanning test with a non-vacuity check, and a §8 v2 proposal built around "one break, once" with must-understand feature tags afterward. The strongest shipped idea is excluding derived state from the file while recording the provenance of the deriver (`metadata.analyzerAdapterId`) so rebuild-on-load cannot silently diverge. The strongest v2 ideas are position-derived ids reconciling byte reproducibility with revision-relatable identity, and `maxAutonomy` as a min-composed, fail-closed authority ceiling that travels inside the artifact. Against that, the implementation drifts from its own spec in several verified places: the §7 fixture table misdescribes the shipped fixtures, a signed file read without a key is reported as corruption, and the version gate is bypassable by a non-numeric `version`.

findings.title: "One break, once": greedy v2, then must-understand feature tags instead of version bumps
findings.whatItIs: The v2 proposal opens with a governing constraint rather than a feature list: a format that breaks twice has taught the market it breaks, so v2 must be the only breaking version and the correct posture is greedy now, conservative afterwards. Two mechanical rules follow: everything in §8 lands together or not at all ("a partial v2 is two breaks wearing one version number"), and after v2 extension happens through a `requires[]` must-understand list in the header — a reader refuses on an unknown feature tag, never on an unknown version, making the version number vestigial by design (the PNG/Matroska model). Three admissible reasons for a v3 are named in advance (broken crypto primitive, a node-model dimension not expressible as a tag, legal requirement), and §8.6 lists what is deliberately excluded with forward pointers to those reasons.
findings.quote: Everything in this section must land together or not at all. A partial v2 is two breaks wearing one version number.
findings.whyItMatters: Most format/schema evolution plans are a backlog with a version number attached. This converts "we'll do the rest later" into a spec violation, and pairs the greedy break with an explicit exclusion list so the greed has a bound. The `requires[]` capability-negotiation move is what removes the need for future breaks at all.

findings.title: Magic identifies the format family; version identifies the revision
findings.whatItIs: v2 files keep the `AIKG` magic. The argument is made entirely through the failure message a stale reader produces: a v1 reader shown a v2 file frames it, reads version 2, and rejects with "format version 2 is newer than this reader supports" — an error naming the real cause. Change the magic and the identical file yields "not a .gai file", which is false, and callers act on that by quarantining intact data. The layering is stated as: magic answers "is this the format?", `requires[]` answers "can I read this particular file?", and only the second may change over time. Provenance: their own first sketch packed the version into the magic (`0x47 0x41 0x49 0x01` = "GAI"+version), and the shipped magic `AIKG` no longer even spells the format's name — kept deliberately for backward compatibility.
findings.quote: A format that reports version skew as a wrong-format error teaches its own tooling to treat upgrades as corruption.
findings.whyItMatters: Rarely written down, and the failure mode is real and destructive: version-in-magic makes every forward-compatibility event indistinguishable from corruption at the recipient, and recipients delete corrupt files. The three-layer split (family / revision / capability) reuses directly for any versioned artifact or schema envelope.

findings.title: Error taxonomy keyed on what the consumer should DO, with version-skew carved out
findings.whatItIs: Every load-path failure carries a stable string `code` plus a `codeClass` from exactly four values: `corruption` (quarantine and try a backup), `version-skew` (NEVER quarantine — the file is fine, the reader is old), `caller` (the call was wrong; retrying identically will not help), `config`. `ERROR_CLASS` is a single `Object.freeze`d total map from 15 codes to those classes, deliberately the only place the relationship is written down, because a second copy is how the consuming app ended up with two divergent classifiers. Consumers branch through exported predicates `isCorruption` / `isVersionSkew` / `isCallerError`, never the code list. It is one error class with a code field, not a subclass per failure, because `instanceof` does not survive duplicated module instances or a bundler that inlines the package (their MCP bundle does exactly that) and does not survive `JSON.stringify` across an IPC/JSON-RPC hop — a string code survives all three.
findings.quote: What a consumer should DO about it. This is the axis that matters.
findings.whyItMatters: The class axis is the insight: cause-shaped error taxonomies force every consumer to re-derive the action, and they get it wrong in the destructive direction (quarantining a valid newer file). The instanceof-vs-code reasoning is a concrete deployment fact most libraries learn only after a bundler eats their error identity.

findings.title: Frozen error messages guarded by a source scan with a negative and a non-vacuity check
findings.whatItIs: Because a shipped downstream consumer classifies load failures by substring-matching message prose, all twelve load-path message strings are declared frozen: codes are additive, messages are never reworded. The guard test reads `gai-reader.ts` and `graph-store.ts` as text and asserts (1) all twelve substrings are still present byte-identical; (2) a negative constraint — extract every `gaiError(...)` message literal by regex and assert none contains the word "signature", because the shipped classifier matches that word and no message contains it today, so adding one would silently reclassify an unrelated failure as corruption; (3) that the extracting regex actually found at least ten messages, so a regex that stops matching cannot turn constraint (2) into a permanent pass. It also asserts the code→class table is total, frozen, and that exactly one code is `version-skew`.
findings.quote: check('the message-literal scan actually found messages — not vacuous', messageLiterals.length >= 10)
findings.whyItMatters: Two rare moves in one file: treating human-readable message text as a versioned API surface with a written freeze policy, and proving a source-scanning assertion is non-vacuous. Most repos ship the scan and never notice when it silently stops finding anything.

findings.title: Authenticate before parse by deriving trailer layout from the caller's key, not the header
findings.whatItIs: A file's signed-ness is declared inside the msgpack header — exactly the bytes you must not deserialize before verifying. The reader breaks the cycle by computing `trailerLen = opts.hmacKey != null ? 4+32 : 4` from the CALLER's intent, so the raw header+body byte range is known before any unpack. Order is: magic bytes → headerLen bounds check against `buffer.length - trailerLen` → additive checksum over the raw ranges → HMAC via `timingSafeEqual` → only then `unpack(headerBuf)` → version gate → downgrade guards → `unpack(bodyBuf)` → structural validation. The changelog records this as a pure reordering with identical HMAC coverage to the writer, hence shippable as a patch with no format change.
findings.quote: We break the cycle by deriving the trailer layout from whether the CALLER supplied a key — not from the header content
findings.whyItMatters: The chicken-and-egg ("the flag telling me whether to verify lives in the thing I must verify") appears in every self-describing signed container, and the usual answer is to parse first and verify later. Moving the layout decision to caller intent is a clean, portable resolution that keeps the deserializer off unauthenticated bytes.

findings.title: Derived state stays out of the file, but the deriver's identity is recorded and fails closed
findings.whatItIs: The format persists nodes and edges only — no TF-IDF index, no embeddings, no adjacency lists — "those are derived and MUST be rebuilt on load", which is what keeps the file a description of memory rather than a snapshot of one engine's internals. But rebuild is only safe if it uses the same tokenisation, so the body's `metadata` carries `analyzerAdapterId` (and `edgePolicyId`), and §5.2 makes honouring it a MUST. An unknown or mismatched analyzer id throws `AnalyzerMismatchError` naming both ids and both remedies rather than defaulting. A parity test pins three historically-divergent rebuild paths (builder, SDK `rebuildIndex`, MCP cache) to identical `documentCount`, identical vocabulary size, and every IDF weight equal to 1e-12, and asserts a legacy graph is re-indexed with the legacy analyzer, not the current default.
findings.quote: documentCount is in the idf numerator for every term, so a different node set means a different score for every query — the same .gai ranked differently depending on which loader opened it. That makes any before/after retrieval measurement a measurement of the loader.
findings.whyItMatters: "Don't persist derived state" is common advice; the missing half — record the identity of the procedure that derives it and fail closed when that identity is unknown — is what stops rebuild-on-load from being a silent-divergence machine. Their measured consequence (every A/B retrieval number was confounded by which loader ran) is the argument.

findings.title: Validate at the deserialization funnel, with the bound taken from the proof not the writer
findings.whatItIs: `fromSerializable` is declared the single funnel every load path passes through, and is where edge weights are validated — because the container's checksum is explicitly a corruption check, not a tamper check, so a file can carry weights no writer would emit. The bound is not the writers' `(0,1]` convention: best-first traversal's path-maximum theorem only needs each hop's multiplier below 1, i.e. `DECAY_FACTOR * w < 1`, so the ceiling is `1/DECAY_FACTOR` (~1.667). The comment explains why the looser bound is correct: files predating a cosine clamp carry 1-ULP overshoots (1.0000000000000002 measured on a real round trip), and refusing to open an existing memory over one ULP would be a data-availability bug introduced in the name of a correctness one. Infinity and NaN are still refused, with the silent failure spelled out (scores rise along a path, heap pops stop arriving in non-increasing order, the dominance test discards strictly better entries).
findings.quote: The bound is the PROOF's bound, not the writers' convention.
findings.whyItMatters: Two transferable moves: put invariant enforcement at the deserialization funnel because integrity checks on the container do not imply semantic validity, and choose the validation bound from what downstream algorithms actually require rather than from what upstream writers happen to emit — otherwise a tightened writer convention retroactively bricks existing files.

findings.title: Conformance declared per layer: L1 container / L2 model / L3 retrieval+authority
findings.whatItIs: Rather than one undifferentiated "conforming", the v2 proposal splits conformance by layer with an explicit rationale: a file format benefits from many independent implementations (that is what proves the bytes are unambiguous) while a retrieval engine does not, because ranking is a design position and two engines that rank differently are not two implementations of one thing. L1 = frame, checksum-verify, reject per §5.1. L2 = round-trip every node, edge, revision and metadata field without loss, plus honour the fail-closed autonomy default. L3 = enforce `maxAutonomy` as a hard gate and implement path-maximum traversal. The status-anxiety countermeasure is explicit: "Most implementations need only L1 or L2, and declaring L2 is a complete claim, not a partial one." Enforcement hook: an implementation declaring L3 while ignoring `maxAutonomy` is non-conforming — without that, the authority section is advisory text.
findings.whyItMatters: Solves the real problem that a spec covering bytes, model, and behaviour cannot have one conformance claim without making it meaningless. The 'L2 is complete, not partial' sentence is what stops a level ladder from becoming a shaming device that pushes everyone to over-claim.

findings.title: maxAutonomy: an authority ceiling stored in the artifact, min-composed and fail-closed
findings.whatItIs: An optional node-metadata field `'L0'|'L1'|'L2'|'L3'` capping how far a stored procedure may act unattended. Five rules give it force: (1) a ceiling is a maximum, never a grant — a host MUST NOT execute above it, MAY execute below, MAY refuse entirely, so the field can only lower authority; (2) it is monotone under composition — a subgraph's effective ceiling is the MINIMUM over its members, so borrowing a skill cannot raise the borrower's ceiling; (3) it survives transport because it is ordinary node metadata carried by the same subgraph envelope as the steps; (4) absence is UNSPECIFIED, not unlimited — a conforming host must treat it as the most restrictive level it supports, "the difference between a ceiling and a suggestion"; (5) a process minting or editing a node MUST NOT set it above the ceiling of the context it runs in. Motivation: in v1 the limit can only live in the holding application, so a memory moved elsewhere arrives with its procedure intact and its constraints absent, and the receiver has no way to discover something is missing.
findings.quote: what proposes an action does not approve its own limits
findings.whyItMatters: Capability ceilings normally live in runtime policy config, which does not travel with the artifact — so a portable skill or procedure silently loses its constraints on transfer. Putting the ceiling in the data, min-composing it, and making absence maximally restrictive is a design I have not seen in a file format, and it generalizes to any transferable agent capability or tool definition.

findings.title: (id,rev) as the carrier merge needs, plus ids allocated from position for reproducibility
findings.whatItIs: Two coupled v2 changes. First, node identity becomes the pair `(id, rev)`: `id` stable for the memory's lifetime and unchanged by content edits, `rev` a monotone per-id counter from 1, exactly one rev is `head`, and "conflict is the state of an id having more than one head". The argument is that without a second slot every merge implementation is forced into one of three wrong moves — overwrite (silent loss), mint a new id for the loser (loses that these are revisions of the same thing), or emit `contradicts` as the self-loop `n1 → n1` (asserts a fact conflicts with itself). Migration needs no external data: every v1 file is the degenerate one-rev case. Second, byte reproducibility comes from allocating ids from corpus coordinates, `id = H(graphId ‖ sourceFile ‖ sectionPath ‖ ordinal)`, explicitly rejecting content-derived ids because they change on every edit and destroy relatability; `contentHash` moves onto the revision instead. The forgotten half is mandated too: a writer MUST accept a `buildInstant` and derive every minted timestamp from it. Known bound: insertions shift later ordinals, affecting a rebuild from source but never an incremental edit.
findings.quote: Every input is a coordinate in the corpus, not a fact about the text... editing a node's content leaves its id untouched, because its position did not move.
findings.whyItMatters: A sharp resolution of a tension most systems resolve badly: content-addressing gives reproducibility but makes revision history unexpressible, while random ids give stability but make two builds of one corpus incomparable. Position-derived identity plus content-addressing at the revision layer gets both, and the `buildInstant` clause names the half that usually sinks reproducibility efforts.

findings.title: Conformance fixtures shipped as bytes, majority malformed, wired into the publish gate
findings.whatItIs: Ten fixture files ship in `spec/fixtures/` (six malformed on purpose) plus a 92-line runner with two primitives: `accepts(file, expect)` and `rejects(file, why)`, where silent acceptance is the recorded failure. Both the runner and the generator open with the same thesis — the useful question about a format reader is not what it accepts but what it REFUSES — and the reason to ship bytes rather than a test suite is that a second implementation in any language can reach the same verdicts. The spec states the bar honestly: a third implementation passing all ten is what would make `.gai` a standard rather than a file layout. `node spec/conformance.mjs` is the last entry in the `test` script, `prepublishOnly` runs lint+build+test, and CI runs the same chain on every push/PR — with a workflow header explaining that before it existed the first verification happened inside the publish job after the tag was already public, leaving a dangling `v0.7.1` tag on origin.
findings.quote: A reader that parses `bad-checksum.gai` without complaint is not conforming, however well it handles valid input.
findings.whyItMatters: Negative fixtures as the primary artifact — and as shipped bytes rather than in-repo assertions — is what makes a format claim falsifiable by a third party. The publish-gate wiring plus the postmortem in the CI header is the process half that makes it stick.

findings.title: Bad fixtures are made by corrupting a good file then RE-FRAMING it, isolating one defect
findings.whatItIs: `make-fixtures.ts` builds one valid file and derives every negative fixture from it by a single surgical mutation, then repairs the envelope so only the intended gate can fail. `bad-checksum.gai` flips one body byte at `4+4+headerLen+8` and leaves the checksum alone. `future-version.gai` unpacks the header, sets `version = 99`, re-packs, and recomputes BOTH `headerLen` and the additive checksum before reassembling — so the file is valid in every other respect and can only fail the version gate. `dangling-edge.gai` unpacks the body, retargets `directedEdges[0].to` to `'no-such-node-id'`, re-packs, recomputes the checksum, and reassembles — so it passes framing and checksum and can only fail the endpoint check. Each `put()` records a one-line expected-outcome note printed at the end of the run.
findings.whyItMatters: Without the re-framing step every mutated fixture fails at the first gate (the checksum) and the suite proves nothing about the later gates — an easy mistake that makes a negative-fixture suite look thorough while testing one branch. The repair-the-envelope discipline is what turns each fixture into a single-defect isolator.

findings.title: A normative Known Weaknesses section, and postmortems promoted into cross-language spec text
findings.whatItIs: The spec carries a weaknesses section opening "a specification that hides its soft spots is worse than one that names them", listing four with mechanism: `contentHash` is 32-bit with the birthday math spelled out (~5% chance of a collision by 20k nodes, ~25% by 50k) and a MUST NOT treat equal hash as equal content; header counts are unauthenticated on unsigned files, hence declared advisory because a reader trusting a count over the body can be made to allocate or truncate incorrectly (verified: rewriting nodeCount to 9999 is accepted and ignored); the checksum is not a MAC; and `accessCount` is mutable state inside an otherwise declarative file, so two files with identical content can rank differently. Separately §4's checksum definition carries a normative warning derived from their own v0.5.7 incident — implementations in signed-32-bit languages must use unsigned right-shift, because a signed mask goes negative above 2^31 — a bug that made every engram over ~17 MB report as corrupt though its bytes were intact, now documented identically in spec, writer, and reader.
findings.quote: The bytes were always valid; only this comparison was wrong.
findings.whyItMatters: Two reusable habits: enumerate a format's soft spots normatively so downstream implementers guard them (their own dedup path violated the 32-bit-hash rule and could hard-delete unrelated content), and promote a reference-implementation postmortem into cross-language spec text plus duplicated inline comments on both sides of the invariant so a later cleanup cannot silently re-break it.

findings.title: One canonical content hash, frozen by the FORMAT; and refuting the reader's wrong inference
findings.whatItIs: Two instances of one discipline. (a) `content-hash.ts` exists solely to collapse three byte-identical private `simpleHash` copies into one, because invariant I5 (`∀n: n.contentHash = h(n.content)`) needs a single `h` to be checkable at all, and because dedup and re-ingest key on the value so a drift would silently split identical memories or merge distinct ones. The algorithm is then frozen not by taste but by the format: changing it changes every contentHash in every existing file, "a format-breaking migration, not a refactor". It also documents that `charCodeAt` walks UTF-16 code units so astral characters contribute two surrogates. (b) §4's confidentiality subsection names the wrong inference before refuting it: the section is titled Integrity, is mostly about HMAC, "and a reader scanning for 'is this protected' finds cryptography and stops" — then states plainly that the body is not encrypted, that HMAC never answers "can a third party read it", that the omission is deliberate because encryption belongs to the layer that knows the trust boundary, and converts that into MUSTs on the caller including a documentation MUST.
findings.quote: The single-file design that makes `.gai` easy to move is exactly what makes an unencrypted one easy to exfiltrate. One file is one copy operation.
findings.whyItMatters: (a) is the general rule that a primitive baked into persisted bytes is frozen by the artifact, not by the codebase, and must have exactly one definition. (b) is a documentation pattern worth copying wholesale: when a design omits a property that adjacent material implies, name the inference the reader is forming and refute it in the same section rather than relying on absence.

antipatterns.title: SPEC §7's fixture table misdescribes the shipped fixtures, and the runner asserts nothing that would catch it
antipatterns.why: The one document telling a second implementer what each conformance fixture contains is wrong about both coverage fixtures, and the suite deliberately omits the assertions that would detect the drift — so an implementation supporting 2 of 15 directed types and 0 of 7 undirected types passes the 'all edge types' gate. Verified by unpacking the shipped bytes.
antipatterns.evidence: SPEC.md:310 claims minimal.gai is '2 nodes, 1 directed edge, 1 undirected edge'; its actual header is {version:1, nodeCount:6, directedEdgeCount:4, undirectedEdgeCount:0}. SPEC.md:312 claims all-edge-types.gai contains 'Every directed and undirected type in §3.3 present at least once'; its body carries 10 directed edges of only two types (contains, precedes) and ZERO undirected edges. spec/conformance.mjs:60-61 calls accepts('minimal.gai') and accepts('all-edge-types.gai') with no expectations object, although the expect mechanism exists at spec/conformance.mjs:29-40 and is used for empty-graph.gai.

antipatterns.title: A signed file read without a key is reported as `corruption`, contradicting SPEC §4/§7
antipatterns.why: SPEC.md:202-206 requires an unverified read to be flagged as unverified, and SPEC.md:311 says signed.gai 'Rejects without it flagged unverified'. Because trailerLen is derived from the caller's key, the 32-byte HMAC is counted as body and the checksum fails first, so the caller gets a code classed 'corruption' — documented as 'safe to quarantine and try a backup'. A consumer obeying the library's own published classification will quarantine a perfectly good signed file whose only defect is a missing key: exactly the destructive misroute the codeClass axis was invented to prevent.
antipatterns.evidence: Measured against dist/: readGai(spec/fixtures/signed.gai) with no key throws code=GAI_CHECKSUM_MISMATCH, codeClass=corruption, 'Invalid .gai file: checksum mismatch'. Mechanism at src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:50-51; the reader acknowledges it at src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:114-117 yet keeps the now-unreachable GAI_HMAC_KEY_MISSING guard at src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:118-120. Class table: src/core/errors.ts:115-124. spec/conformance.mjs:73-88 tests only correct-key and wrong-key, never no-key.

antipatterns.title: The version gate is bypassable by a non-numeric `version`, and is set one version ahead of anything implemented
antipatterns.why: The `typeof header.version === 'number' &&` conjunct turns the single mandatory §5.1 gate into a no-op for any header whose version is absent or not a number — the exact 'read it as if it were this one' outcome the reader's own comment condemns. Separately the reader claims support for version 2 while the writer emits 1 and §8 states nothing of v2 is implemented, so a genuine v2 file (with (id,rev) identity and maxAutonomy semantics) would be accepted and misread.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:103 guard; src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:7 GAI_VERSION_SUPPORTED = 2 vs src/core/constants.ts:9 GAI_VERSION = 1; SPEC.md:334 'Status: PROPOSAL. Nothing here is implemented'; SPEC.md:78 says the format version is '2 for this document' while every written file says 1. Measured on reframed copies of minimal.gai with recomputed checksums: version="99" (string) ACCEPTED, version missing ACCEPTED, version=-1 ACCEPTED, version=2 ACCEPTED, version=99 rejected (control).

antipatterns.title: Only nine failure shapes are coded; other malformed bodies escape as uncoded TypeErrors
antipatterns.why: readGai type-asserts the unpacked body instead of validating it, so a checksum-valid but structurally wrong body crashes inside fromSerializable with a message carrying no code and neither frozen prefix. The shipped consumer classifier quoted in the library's own comments then treats it as non-corruption and the engram silently disappears from the picker — the literal incident the code system was built to close, still reachable. Unsigned bodies are attacker-modifiable by design since SPEC.md:195 calls the checksum trivially forgeable.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:125-130 (unpack plus an `as` assertion, no validation); src/core/graph/graph-store.ts:95 trusts data.nodes.map; src/core/errors.ts:49-56 documents the consumer classifier and the silent-disappearance incident. Measured with recomputed checksums: body.nodes='x' -> TypeError 'data.nodes.map is not a function' (code undefined); body={} and body=7 -> TypeError 'data.directedEdges is not iterable' (code undefined).

antipatterns.title: The declared 'single funnel' enforces one structural invariant and not the other
antipatterns.why: graph-store.ts advertises fromSerializable as the funnel every load path passes through and puts the edge-weight invariant there, but the dangling-edge check — an explicit §5.1 MUST-reject — lives only in readGai. The SQLite loader and the public fromSerializable export therefore accept a graph the file reader refuses, so what counts as a valid graph depends on which door it came through, and the confident doc comment makes the gap harder to notice.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/graph/graph-store.ts:35-56 ('the single funnel every load path goes through — readGai, fromBuffer, the SQLite loader, and the public fromSerializable export'); the endpoint check exists only at src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:150-159; a repo-wide grep for GAI_DANGLING_EDGE hits only src/core/errors.ts:99,126 and gai-reader.ts:152,157; src/core/persistence/sqlite-store.ts:251 returns fromSerializable(serializable) with no endpoint validation.

antipatterns.title: `writeGaiAtomic` is triplicated byte-for-byte and no copy fsyncs the parent directory
antipatterns.why: The repo centralized simpleHash into one module precisely because 'three copies of a hash function are three chances for one to drift' — the identical argument applies to three copies of the crash-safety primitive. All three do open(tmp,0o600) -> write -> fsync(fd) -> close -> rename, omitting the directory fsync that makes the rename survive power loss; fixing that now needs three edits, and any one missed leaves a silently non-durable write path under a comment claiming crash safety.
antipatterns.evidence: src/sdk/index.ts:357-367; src/mcp/tools/export.ts:46-56; src/mcp/tools/update_graph.ts:115-123 (byte-identical bodies, none opens or fsyncs dirname(filePath)). Contrast the stated rationale at src/core/graph/content-hash.ts:9-12 and the crash-safety claim at CHANGELOG.md:1132-1139.

surveys.summary: This territory is a disciplined evidence culture built on a deliberately framework-free test substrate: 26 plain `tsx` scripts that print ok/FAIL and exit non-zero, chained with `&&` in one npm script, plus a `.gai` conformance suite, a packaged-artifact verifier, and a benchmark evidence bundle that verifies itself. The error system's real contribution is not codes but a CLASS axis above them — corruption / version-skew / caller / config — with a single frozen code→class table, because the consumer's question is "what do I do about it", and because a prefix-matching consumer would otherwise quarantine a perfectly good file written by a newer writer. The tests read like incident reports: nearly every guard names the defect that produced it, every scan carries a non-vacuity assertion, and several record measured mutation results ("deleting the Giki gate was caught 0 times in 10 runs"). The benchmark side is the strongest part — an evidence bundle whose verifier recomputes filenames, deltas and even prose "+N.N point" claims from the raw rows; a manifest that grades the provenance of every reproducing command; a retroactively added `--traversal-order fifo` flag so archived measurements stay reproducible after a default changed; and a README flying a grey `re-measuring` badge that refuses to quote a current headline. The weaknesses are all unenforced-claim weaknesses: the evidence verifier is not in CI, the tests are never typechecked, and the doc surfaces with no checker have visibly drifted.

findings.title: Error CLASS above error code: version-skew is not corruption
findings.whatItIs: Beyond a stable code enum, every code maps through one frozen `ERROR_CLASS` record to one of four consumer-actionable classes — `corruption` (quarantine, try a backup), `version-skew` (NEVER quarantine, the file is fine and the reader is old), `caller` (retrying unchanged will fail identically), `config`. Three 3-line predicates (`isCorruption`/`isVersionSkew`/`isCallerError`) branch on the class, not the code. The design note states the axis: "the question a consumer actually asks is not 'which error' but 'what do I do about it'". The table is deliberately the only place the relationship is written, because a second copy is how the consuming app ended up with two divergent classifiers.
findings.quote: `Invalid .gai file: format version N is newer than this reader supports` DOES contain `Invalid .gai`, so a consumer routing that prefix to "corrupt" would QUARANTINE A PERFECTLY GOOD FILE written by a newer version.
findings.whyItMatters: Most error taxonomies stop at a code, which just moves the string-matching one level up: the consumer still has to know which of 15 codes means 'safe to destroy the file'. Naming the recovery action as a first-class, frozen, exhaustively-tested axis is what actually lets a downstream harness write correct recovery logic, and the version-skew-vs-corruption split is a real data-loss bug class most persistence layers get wrong.

findings.title: One error class carrying a string code — deliberately NOT subclass-per-failure
findings.whatItIs: `GraphnosisError extends Error` with readonly `code` and `codeClass` fields, constructed via a `gaiError(code, message)` factory that passes the message through unchanged. The documented reason for rejecting one subclass per failure is mechanical: `instanceof` does not survive duplicated module instances (two copies in a dependency tree, or an esbuild bundle that inlines the package — "the app's MCP bundle does exactly that"), and it does not survive `JSON.stringify` across an IPC or JSON-RPC boundary, whereas a string field does. A test asserts the JSON survivability directly.
findings.quote: `instanceof` does not survive duplicated module instances ... whereas a string code does. It also survives `JSON.stringify` across an IPC or JSON-RPC boundary, which `instanceof` cannot
findings.whyItMatters: Any library that crosses a bundler, a worker, an MCP/JSON-RPC boundary, or ends up duplicated in a lockfile hits this. The reasoning is a checklist for choosing between tagged-union-style discriminants and prototype-based error hierarchies, and it argues for data over nominal typing at exactly the boundary where nominal typing silently fails.

findings.title: Frozen message strings as a compatibility surface, with a negative-word test
findings.whatItIs: Because a shipped consumer substring-matches error prose, the messages are declared frozen and additive-only ("add a code, never reword a message"). A test reads the source text of the two producing modules, asserts twelve message substrings are still present byte-identically, then regex-extracts only the message literals out of `gaiError(...)` call sites and asserts that none contains the word `signature` — the shipped classifier matches that word and no message contains it today, so adding it would silently reclassify an unrelated failure as corruption. Comments mentioning the word are allowed; only reachable strings matter.
findings.quote: THE MESSAGES ARE FROZEN. Every message string on the load path is now load-bearing for at least one already-shipped consumer.
findings.whyItMatters: It is a concrete technique for the awkward migration window where you have shipped a better contract but old consumers are still on the bad one: keep the bad contract mechanically pinned by a test until they move, and encode the *negative* constraints too. The literal-extraction regex (so comments are exempt) is the detail that makes it usable rather than annoying.

findings.title: Non-vacuity clauses on every guard, plus recorded mutation results
findings.whatItIs: Nearly every scan, fixture or differential ships with a companion assertion that it exercises anything at all — "the message-literal scan actually found messages — not vacuous", "the two orders genuinely DIFFER on this graph", "the random graphs DO exercise the defect", "fixture actually contains section nodes", plus explicit negative controls. On top of that, guards are neutralised and the result is written into the comment with numbers: three separate BFS edge-direction guards exist because "a fixture that covers only the outgoing one passes with the other two guards deleted. (Measured: it did.)", and one retirement case exists because without it "deleting the Giki gate was caught 0 times in 10 runs".
findings.quote: a fixture that covers only the outgoing one passes with the other two guards deleted. (Measured: it did.)
findings.whyItMatters: This is manual mutation testing with the result committed as prose, at a density I have not seen in a real repo. It converts 'we have a test for that' into 'we measured that this test fails when the guard is removed', and the non-vacuity clause makes a whole class of silently-green tests impossible. Cheap to adopt: it is one extra `check()` per scan.

findings.title: Packaged-artifact verifier: pack, install, import every export — with a canary
findings.whatItIs: A 151-line node script that `npm pack`s, installs the tarball into a fresh temp package with no workspace or path aliases, generates a probe that dynamically imports every non-JSON key of `pkg.exports` by its public specifier, asserts the root entry exports ≥20 symbols ("a dist that resolves but exports nothing is the subtle version of broken"), and greps the installed tree for unrewritten `@/` aliases. It refuses to run when `dist/` is missing (exit 2) so it cannot pass by verifying nothing, and it ends by writing a `__canary.js` containing an alias import, re-running the grep, and asserting the check FINDS it — a positive control for the guard itself.
findings.quote: Positive control: the check above must be able to FIND an alias when one is present, or "clean" means nothing. Same discipline as the conformance harness — a guard reported without its mutation is unproven.
findings.whyItMatters: It closes the exact gap most repos have: the whole suite imports through path aliases into `src/`, so nothing ever exercises what npm ships. The grep-exit-code note (grep exits 1 on no match, which is the good case; treating non-zero as failure inverts the check) is a bug they hit and documented, and the canary makes the negative result meaningful.

findings.title: Adversarial fixture construction: engineer the fixture against the named blind spot
findings.whatItIs: Fixtures are designed backwards from the specific way the test could pass while proving nothing, with the reasoning written down. The path-maximum suite's 2000-trial random-graph differential (deterministic mulberry32 vs brute-force enumeration of every walk) spreads edge weights because "a uniform-weight graph cannot exhibit the defect, which is exactly why the synthetic corpus showed zero difference", makes a third of edges undirected because "a differential that skips a whole branch proves nothing about it", and uses multiple seeds at differing scores because with one seed "a deleted heapify loop would pass every assertion". The ingest-determinism suite makes the same move about identity: hand-authored node ids never exercise the nanoid-minted ids production uses, so it builds the corpus twice, asserts the two id-spaces are disjoint, compares evidence by CONTENT, and tests the tie-break comparator directly after documenting two earlier fixtures that were provably inert ("passed 20/20 against a surgically reverted comparator").
findings.quote: a tie-break on node id passes a fixture test and still reorders evidence in production. That is exactly what shipped: on a 40-question sample, evidence ORDER differed on 21/40 and the evidence SET on 6/40 between two builds inside one single-threaded process.
findings.whyItMatters: Two transferable rules fall out: (1) a hand-built fixture whose identifiers differ from production identifiers cannot test anything keyed on identity, and (2) a randomized differential must be audited for the branches and value distributions it never reaches. Both are the difference between a suite that catches the bug and one that shipped it.

findings.title: An evidence bundle that verifies itself — filenames, deltas, and prose claims
findings.whatItIs: `benchmarks/evidence/` ships eight sanitized per-question JSONL result files plus a 96-line verifier that (1) SHA-256s every file against `checksums.txt`, (2) parses the score out of each FILENAME and recomputes it from the rows, failing on >0.05 disagreement, (3) recomputes five asserted deltas from a table where each entry names the two arms it is a difference OF, and (4) regexes every `+N.N point` claim out of the manifest's prose descriptions and fails if the number is not in that delta table. It exists because the manifest once claimed +11.8 where its own rows gave 78.00−64.60=13.40 and nothing was checking. I ran it: exit 0, all 26 checks pass.
findings.quote: 13.2 is the TF-IDF graph-vs-flat delta (62.2 - 49.0) and comparing 78.0 against the same flat arm instead would move two variables at once — retrieval mode AND embeddings — and produce a number that means nothing.
findings.whyItMatters: It makes published numbers falsifiable by machine instead of by trust, including the arithmetic in the surrounding prose. The pairing discipline — every delta declares its two arms so a one-variable comparison is structurally enforced — is the part that generalizes to any A/B or ablation reporting.

findings.title: Provenance grading per run, plus a reproducibility flag added retroactively
findings.whatItIs: Each run in the manifest carries file, score, sha256, the exact reproducing command, a description, and a `command_provenance` field with an honesty grade — "exact — confirmed by author", "confirmed — author-attested", or an admission that the harness did not record the env var that identifies the arm ("a harness gap, now fixed for future runs"). Separately, when SDK 0.10.0 changed the default traversal frontier, they added a `--traversal-order fifo` flag whose sole purpose is to restore pre-0.10.0 semantics, retrofitted it into every archived command, and stated the incomparability boundary: the change alters retrieval on ~9% of real multi-session queries, and "these are NOT 0.10.0 numbers".
findings.quote: The flag did not exist when these runs were made; it was added in 0.10.0 precisely so a pre-0.10.0 measurement stays reproducible.
findings.whyItMatters: Two ideas worth stealing: grading how confident you are that a recorded command is the command that produced a number (instead of silently presenting all of them as equally solid), and treating 'old measurements must remain reproducible' as a reason to ship a compatibility flag when you change a default. The alternative — silently invalidating your entire published history — is what almost everyone does.

findings.title: The "re-measuring" badge: refusing to quote a headline the code cannot support
findings.whatItIs: The README's benchmark badge reads `LongMemEval — re-measuring` in grey, not a number, and the Benchmark section says a current headline figure is deliberately not quoted because this release line changed retrieval. The four published arms are shown with the caveat "read them as evidence that the ablations separate, not as a current score". `benchmarks.md` carries a matching banner ("No run in this log is current") and calls its own 78.00% best "the top of a distribution rather than a stable level", since the same configuration spans 72.8–76.4%. A comparability-boundary section measures sampling noise at ±0.3pp from three same-config replicates, prescribes the control arm needed to re-anchor, and flags a second unpinned input: a 25,269-entry enrichment cache generated before temperature pinning.
findings.quote: A current headline figure is deliberately not quoted here. ... The number returns when the run does.
findings.whyItMatters: This is a reusable pattern for shipping honest metrics: a status-valued badge instead of a possibly-stale number, an explicit staleness banner on the history file, single-run results labelled as distribution samples rather than levels, and an in-place `> **Corrected.**` block when a comparison turns out to be wrong (they retract a comparator that was an ablation arm rather than a baseline). It costs nothing and it is the opposite of what most benchmark READMEs do.

findings.title: The measuring instrument identifies, defines and unit-tests itself
findings.whatItIs: The free retrieval-recall harness emits a report stamped with `instrument` name+version, the SHA-256 of its OWN source file, `argv`, recorded env, dataset path (deliberately relative, so it does not leak the operator's home dir) and dataset SHA-256 — plus a `definitions` block that ships the metric semantics (micro vs macro recall, any vs complete coverage, what a session/turn unit is, and the policy for unannotated questions) inside the artifact. A `--self-test` flag runs unit tests of the metric functions themselves, independent of the system under test, and the harness refuses `--out` paths under `data/` because the evidence directory is read-only. The paired comparison tool prints both reports' instrument SHAs and stamps ` MISMATCH` when they differ.
findings.quote: Every JSON report stamps the harness source SHA-256, argv, and dataset SHA-256 so two arms can be checked as measurements from one instrument revision.
findings.whyItMatters: It answers 'are these two numbers even comparable?' mechanically instead of by memory, and it puts the metric's definition where the number is rather than in a doc that drifts. The `--self-test` idea — the instrument carries tests of its own scoring functions — is the piece that separates 'the system regressed' from 'the metric changed'.

findings.title: An ablation wired in as a CI gate, with a faithfulness check on the shipped path
findings.whatItIs: `tests/ablation-scoring/maxwins-vs-additive.ts` runs in `npm test`. It compares the shipped max-score-wins traversal against an inline additive transcription in which only three score-update sites differ (each marked `// <<ADDITIVE>>`), pins the real arm to `traversalOrder: 'fifo'` so the two arms differ in exactly one variable, and then runs the REAL traverser through its gated `GNOSIS_SCORE_RULE=additive` branch and requires it to match the inline reference to 1e-9. It ends by asserting four named invariants and exiting non-zero: the gated branch is faithful, max-wins keeps an in-degree-15 popularity hub dead last, additive promotes it, and the answer node outranks the hub under max-wins. A 20-line comment documents the time the transcription went stale, with the arithmetic proving no rank moved.
findings.quote: Measured: on this fixture both orders give identical max-wins scores, so pinning changes no number here — it restores control by construction rather than by coincidence.
findings.whyItMatters: Two mechanisms generalize: an experiment can be a regression gate if you name the invariants it demonstrates and exit non-zero on them, and any reference/oracle implementation kept alongside production code needs a faithfulness assertion or it silently rots (which is exactly what happened here and was caught).

findings.title: Conformance fixtures shipped for second implementations; refusal is the contract
findings.whatItIs: `spec/` ships 11 committed `.gai` fixtures — half deliberately malformed — plus a 91-line runner that imports the reader from `dist/`, not `src/`. The malformations are byte-surgery on a real written file: one flipped body byte after the header, a 60% truncation, `0xffffff` in the headerLen slot, a msgpack header rewritten to version 99 with the additive checksum RECOMPUTED so the file is otherwise valid, and a directed edge repointed at a missing node id with the checksum recomputed. A generator script (`make-fixtures.ts`) reproduces them all, and the signed fixture ships with its key literally named `conformance-fixture-key-do-not-use-in-production`.
findings.quote: the useful question about a format reader is not what it accepts but what it REFUSES. A reader that parses `bad-checksum.gai` without complaint is not conforming, however well it handles valid input.
findings.whyItMatters: Framing a format spec's test suite around refusal, and shipping the fixtures so an independent implementation can reach the same verdicts, is the difference between a format spec and a format description. Recomputing the checksum after each corruption is the craft detail — it forces the reader to fail for the intended reason rather than tripping over the integrity check first.

findings.title: Refusal design: the validator returns the error, so batches are atomic
findings.whatItIs: `refusalFor(...)` returns the coded `GraphnosisError` a write WOULD throw, or null — never throwing itself — so the batch path can validate every entry before mutating anything; a bad entry refuses the whole batch, writes nothing, does not bump the graph version, and the message enumerates every failing entry. Values outside range are refused rather than silently clamped (NaN is refused, not turned into something plausible), and the messages point at the correct API instead of describing the violation ("Use clampConfidence() if saturating is what you meant"; "Zero is reserved for retirement; to stop serving this memory call deleteNode(), which leaves a tombstone"). The retirement marker `RETIRED_CONFIDENCE = 0` sits deliberately below the legal floor `CONFIDENCE_MIN = 0.01` so a live value can never forge it, and a test asserts that ordering directly.
findings.quote: Extracted so the batch path can check every entry before mutating anything.
findings.whyItMatters: Returning the error instead of throwing gives all-or-nothing batch semantics for free with no transaction machinery, and turns the same validator into a dry-run API. The reserved-sentinel-below-the-legal-floor trick is a clean way to make an audit marker unforgeable by ordinary writes, and asserting the constant ordering (`RETIRED < MIN`) in a test pins it against a future 'let's allow 0'.

findings.title: CI = exactly the release chain, and the irreversible-step gate runs last
findings.whatItIs: `ci.yml` was created after a dangling public `v0.7.1` tag existed with no CHANGELOG section, no npm version and no GitHub Release, and its stated design rule is to run the exact chain `prepublishOnly` runs (lint:lib && build:lib && test) on every push and PR, before a tag is involved. The explicit build step is kept even though `npm ci` already builds via `prepare`, because "if `prepare` ever stops running it, silence would look like success". The publish workflow gates on a non-empty `## v<TAG>` CHANGELOG section (reused verbatim as the GitHub Release body, so the check and the artifact cannot diverge) and on tag == package.json version — placed LAST, immediately before `npm publish`, so it also catches anything earlier in the job that rewrote package.json. Publishing uses npm OIDC trusted publishing with no NPM_TOKEN.
findings.quote: A version number was spent to discover a problem this workflow would have caught for free.
findings.whyItMatters: Defining CI as 'literally the release script, run early' removes the class of failures where the release path is the only untested path. And the ordering rule — put the cheap identity check immediately before the irreversible step, not at the top of the job — is a small, general insight about gate placement in publish pipelines that npm's non-retractability makes expensive to learn the other way.

antipatterns.title: Conformance asserts that it threw, never why — so the error-class system is unused at the format boundary
antipatterns.why: `rejects()` catches anything and calls it a pass. The repo built a whole stable code/class system for precisely this question and does not use it here, so a second implementation that rejects every malformed file with one generic error would 'conform'. Proof it matters: I ran the suite and `truncated.gai` is rejected as `Invalid .gai file: checksum mismatch`, not `truncated` — `GAI_TRUNCATED` is never observed by conformance at all, and nothing notices that the fixture named for it exercises a different code.
antipatterns.evidence: spec/conformance.mjs:46-55 (the `rejects` helper); spec/conformance.mjs:67 (`rejects('truncated.gai', 'body cut short')`); live output: `ok truncated.gai — rejected: Invalid .gai file: checksum mismatch`; src/core/errors.ts:92 (GAI_TRUNCATED in the class table)

antipatterns.title: The conformance fixtures contain zero undirected edges — half the dual graph is untested
antipatterns.why: Running the suite prints `minimal.gai — 6 nodes, 4+0 edges` and `all-edge-types.gai — 10 nodes, 10+0 edges`. Both fixtures are described as covering both edge layers / 'broad edge-type coverage' and neither contains a single undirected edge. The product's entire thesis is the dual graph, and the undirected dangling-edge branch plus the frozen messages `Invalid .gai file: undirected edge ` and `Invalid graph: undirected edge ` have no fixture behind them — they are pinned as strings but never executed.
antipatterns.evidence: spec/make-fixtures.ts:45 ('parses; small graph with both edge layers'); spec/make-fixtures.ts:62 ('all-edge-types.gai', 'broad edge-type coverage'); live conformance output (4+0 and 10+0 edges); src/core/format/gai-reader.ts:157; tests/unit/error-codes.test.ts:110-113

antipatterns.title: The self-verifying evidence bundle is verified by nobody — it is not in npm test or CI
antipatterns.why: `verify.mjs` says of itself "Exits non-zero on any disagreement, so it can gate a release", and the README tells readers to run it, but it appears in neither `npm test` (package.json:61), nor `prepublishOnly` (package.json:46), nor any workflow step. The single best artifact in this territory only runs when a human remembers, which is the same failure mode that produced the +11.8-vs-+13.4 error it was written to prevent.
antipatterns.evidence: benchmarks/evidence/verify.mjs:12-13; README.md:436; package.json:61; package.json:46; .github/workflows/ci.yml:29-74 (no verify.mjs step)

antipatterns.title: 9,300 lines of tests are never typechecked — tsx strips types, and no tsc --noEmit exists
antipatterns.why: `npm test` runs all 26 suites through `tsx`, which erases types without checking them; `tsconfig.build.json` excludes `**/*.test.ts`; there is no `typecheck` script and no `tsc --noEmit` in any workflow. The suites lean heavily on `as unknown as KnowledgeGraph` casts to build fixtures, so drift between a fixture and the real type is invisible — and one test explicitly claims compile-time protection ('if any of them stopped being re-exported, the file would not compile') that nothing enforces.
antipatterns.evidence: package.json:61 (26 × tsx); package.json:38-62 (no typecheck script); tsconfig.build.json:39-41 (excludes *.test.ts); tests/unit/traversal-determinism.test.ts:61 (`as unknown as KnowledgeGraph`); tests/unit/confidence-primitive.test.ts:458-461

antipatterns.title: Documentation drift precisely where no checker exists: the app page, AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md
antipatterns.why: The shipped product page tells users .gai is 'typically 40-60% smaller' than JSON while the repo's own bench artifact records 88% of JSON (12% smaller), and states the magic bytes are `47 41 49 01 = "GAI"` when GAI_MAGIC is `AIKG`. AGENTS.md still documents ~1%/day confidence decay and soft-delete at confidence 0.1, both of which the code retired (decay is opt-in; retirement drives confidence to 0). CONTRIBUTING.md still calls the format `.aikg`. The contrast is the lesson: the evidence bundle has a verifier that binds prose to data, and the surfaces with no verifier are exactly the ones that rotted.
antipatterns.evidence: src/app/view-gai/page.tsx:224 vs benchmarks/dual-graph-and-recall.json:57-58; src/app/view-gai/page.tsx:146 vs src/core/constants.ts:8; AGENTS.md:43,55 vs tests/unit/reflect-no-decay.test.ts:15-19 and src/core/graph/retirement.ts:135; CONTRIBUTING.md:58

antipatterns.title: A serial `&&` runner with 25 hand-rolled harnesses: one red hides the rest
antipatterns.why: package.json:61 chains 27 invocations with `&&`, so the first failing suite aborts the remaining ~20 and there is no aggregate report — diagnosing two independent breakages costs a full re-run each. 27 files declare their own `let failures = 0` and 25 declare their own `check()` with subtly different output formats. The zero-dependency instinct is defensible; the absence of a 20-line shared harness module is not, and the drift already shows (verify-package.mjs still says 'All 24 gated test suites' when there are 26 plus conformance).
antipatterns.evidence: package.json:61; scripts/verify-package.mjs:7; tests/unit/error-codes.test.ts:33-37 vs tests/unit/traversal-determinism.test.ts:21-29 vs spec/conformance.mjs:24-26 (three different check() shapes); `grep -rln 'let failures = 0' tests/ spec/ scripts/ benchmarks/` → 27 files

surveys.summary: This territory is a small, unusually well-argued epistemic state machine over graph nodes. Its organising insight is that four axes routinely conflated by memory systems — existence, liveness (the owner retracted it), currency (the fact's own time window closed), and weight (ranking confidence) — must each get their own field, own write path, and own refusal rules, because every conflation produces a specific silent data-loss bug. The concrete mechanisms: edit() and supersede() are literally the same operation differing only in the reason string; the tombstone carries a two-valued reason ('delete' | 'supersede') whose entire job is telling a later re-ingest of the unchanged source file whether to restore the content; confidence is a ranking weight never allowed to encode liveness (0 is reserved as the tombstone marker, live nodes floor at 0.01); contradictions are reported to the owner and never resolved by the engine; bulk forgetting has a dry run that shares the real code path. The source comments are effectively a defect log — nearly every guard carries the incident, the measurement, the rejected alternative, and what breaks if removed — and the tests are written so removing a guard turns a named check red. The weakest parts are the reflection engine (a second, incompatible contradiction detector that appears unable to fire on real corrections, mutates the graph during "detection", and never consults retirement) and the MCP surface, which exposes none of this to an agent.

findings.title: edit() is literally supersede(); the only difference is caller intent carried in the reason
findings.whatItIs: applyEdit validates its arguments, refuses a retired target, then tail-calls applySupersede. A correction always retires the prior node, mints a NEW node with the corrected content, and records the relationship as a `supersedes` directed edge (weight 1.0, evidence = the human reason). The API consequences were accepted rather than hidden: affectedNodeIds now returns the NEW node id, node count grows by one per edit, and nodesModified is permanently 0 for edits.
findings.quote: An edit and a supersede are the same operation on the graph: the prior belief is retired and readable, the corrected one is a new node, and a `supersedes` edge records the relationship. The only difference is the caller's intent, so the reason carries that and the mechanism is shared.
findings.whyItMatters: In-place edit destroyed the prior belief, and the comment names two non-obvious downstream failures it caused: a later re-ingest of the unchanged source silently UNDID the correction (nothing marked it), and node identity became ambiguous so 'which facts were live at time T' was unanswerable. Collapsing edit into supersede removes an entire class of write that can lose information, at the cost of one node per correction.

findings.title: The retirement reason IS a re-ingest policy: 'delete' is restorable, 'supersede' is not
findings.whatItIs: Tombstones carry metadata.retiredBy: 'delete' | 'supersede'. blocksReingest(node, now, supersededIds) returns true for live nodes, expired-not-retired nodes, and supersede tombs, but FALSE for delete tombs — so the ingest dedup index only contains nodes eligible to suppress incoming identical content. Forgetting a source then re-adding the file restores the content; superseding a fact and re-syncing the file that still carries the old text does not resurrect it.
findings.quote: delete — the user asked to forget this content. Re-adding the source SHOULD restore it: forgetting is not a permanent ban on a string. supersede — the user asserted the stored fact was WRONG and replaced it. Re-syncing the unchanged source must NOT resurrect it; the file still carrying the old text is precisely why the correction existed.
findings.whyItMatters: Almost every memory system models deletion as one thing. This shows deletion has two meanings that differ only in what a later sync should do, that the difference is invisible in any confidence/score representation (the previous test was `confidence > 0.1` and could not tell them apart — it re-created corrected-away facts as live 0.9-confidence nodes outranking their own tombstones), and that it must therefore be a first-class enum on the tombstone consulted by the ingest path.

findings.title: Retirement hardens and never softens: the reason merges up, the instant never moves
findings.whatItIs: retireNode returns a boolean saying whether THIS call actually retired the node. Superseding an already-retired node writes retiredBy = 'supersede' unconditionally (the stricter reason wins) but only stamps instant-bearing markers (deletedAt/deleteReason) when retireNode returned true. applyDelete is the mirror: it never stamps delete markers over an existing retirement. applySupersede also captures supersededIds BEFORE creating its own supersedes edge, or the node would land in its own set and end up retired at every instant in history including the audit hatch.
findings.quote: Superseding a node that was ALREADY retired ... leaves the original retirement instant alone — lineage is history — but the reason must harden to 'supersede'. It is the stricter of the two ... The hardening is unconditional; the instant-bearing markers are not.
findings.whyItMatters: Gives a total, order-independent merge rule for lifecycle state under repeated or concurrent operations: strictness is a lattice join, history is immutable. Without it, a routine delete over a supersede tomb downgrades the reason, which flips blocksReingest to false and resurrects corrected-away content on the next source sync.

findings.title: Liveness comes from markers; confidence is a ranking weight in both directions
findings.whatItIs: isRetired requires an administrative marker (retiredBy, or legacy deletedAt/forgottenAt/supersedes-edge+validUntil) AND the clock; isExpired is the complement — validUntil reached with NO administrative marker. Retired nodes are excluded from every retrieval stage; expired-not-retired nodes stay eligible and are damped x0.3 in traversal. Confidence never decides liveness: RETIRED_CONFIDENCE = 0 is a pure audit marker and CONFIDENCE_MIN = 0.01 is the floor a LIVE node may be given, so a tomb and a decayed memory can never collide.
findings.quote: Before this split, `isRetired` was `validUntil != null && validUntil <= now`. That treated every expired temporal fact as forgotten — "my parking permit expires 30 June" vanished from prompts as though the owner had retracted it.
findings.whyItMatters: Two distinct facts (the owner retracted this / this fact's own window closed) were sharing one field, and the conflation silently deleted time-bounded facts from prompts. The numeric reservation (0 for tombs, 0.01 floor for live) is what lets an auditor read a node's confidence and know which class it is in — and it is why writing 0 onto a live node is refused as forgery of the tombstone marker.

findings.title: setConfidence: a write that neither mints nor retires, with a receipt read back from the graph
findings.whatItIs: setNodeConfidence(graph, nodeId, value, reason, now) changes exactly one field of one node — same id, content, contentHash, entities, edges, createdAt, liveness — and returns ConfidenceChange {nodeId, previous, applied, changed, reason, at} whose `applied` is read back FROM THE NODE after the assignment, not echoed from the argument. The audit stamp (confidenceSetAt/From/To/Reason plus a confidenceWrites counter) lives on the node rather than in an op-log, so record and state are the same artifact and round-trip together through .gai and SQLite. A no-op write is still recorded with changed:false because 'reviewed, unchanged' is a real event.
findings.quote: This package has no op-log, and adding one for this operation alone would make things worse rather than better: a log that records confidence writes and is blind to the four correction paths is a second source of truth that is authoritative for one operation and wrong about the rest.
findings.whyItMatters: The motivating incident is a general law about API surface: the host had no primitive for 'weigh this a bit higher', so it emulated reinforcement as edit(id, sameContent, 'reinforce') — which, once edit became a supersede, minted a duplicate and retired the original on EVERY recall, and (because the content came from a truncated read) silently shortened the memory each time. 'A primitive that does not exist gets emulated, and the emulation is worse than the gap.' The read-back receipt is the anti-divergence mechanism for any audited mutation.

findings.title: Throw-vs-return chosen per operation by how ignorable a refusal is; batches are atomic
findings.whatItIs: Corrections return {applied:0, errors:[...]} and never throw — defensible because they run in batches. Confidence writes throw a GraphnosisError with a stable code and codeClass:'caller', because there is no batch to protect and a returned error is ignorable by doing nothing. setNodeConfidences validates every entry before writing anything: one bad entry means nothing is written, the throw names EVERY failing entry, a repeated node id is refused rather than last-write-wins, and the whole batch bumps metadata.version exactly once.
findings.quote: A returned error is ignorable by doing nothing, and doing nothing is what callers do.
findings.whyItMatters: It replaces a religious 'errors as values vs exceptions' argument with an operational one and documents the observed downstream failure for each shape (a consumer wrapped the never-throwing edit() in try/catch and discarded the errors that are always returned, reporting a correction that never happened as a success). The all-or-nothing batch rationale is the sharp part: a partial batch can only be reported as a per-entry array, which is the ignorable shape the module exists to avoid.

findings.title: Preview-before-forget: the dry run is the same code path, and the blast radius was measured
findings.whatItIs: forgetByTopic takes {dryRun?: boolean}; on dry run it collects the same nodeIds through the same loop and predicates but skips the mutation and returns {forgotten: 0, nodeIds}. previewForgetTopic is a thin wrapper. Matching was also changed from raw case-insensitive substring to a word-boundary regex built by escaping the topic and bounding it with Unicode non-word classes on both sides.
findings.quote: Measured on an 18,968-node graph: forgetTopic('aster') retired 2,151 nodes, 127 of them only because an unrelated word was 'Pilaster'. forgetTopic('data') retired 1,546 ... That is an unbounded authority over a user's memories.
findings.whyItMatters: Two transferable moves. (1) A preview that reuses the operation's own predicate cannot drift from the operation; a parallel estimator can. (2) Wide destructive operations get framed as a governance/authority problem, not a UX nicety — the JSDoc had also CLAIMED it tokenized like the query engine while the code substring-matched, which is how the blast radius stayed invisible.

findings.title: Contradictions are surfaced for owner adjudication and deliberately under-detected
findings.whatItIs: Every append* returns AppendResult.contradictions and the graph is not modified: the old node is not retired, rewritten, or merged. Ingest detection requires two or more shared STRONG entities (structural weak entities — bare years, ISO/slash dates, money, percentages, sub-4-char tokens — are stripped by regex), both passages over 60 characters, and an explicit strong correction marker; weak discourse markers ('however', 'in fact') were removed as the dominant false-positive source. The whole-graph entity index is built in one pass restricted to entities the new batch touches, replacing an O(entities_new x N) scan that caused a multi-GB ingest heap spike.
findings.quote: Nothing is resolved for you. ... You are told there is a conflict and you decide: supersede, keep both, or reject. A vector store has no place to put that decision, so it silently keeps both and lets ranking pick a winner per query. ... A false contradiction is worse than a missed one.
findings.whyItMatters: The precision-over-recall calibration is stated as a rule and then implemented as concrete thresholds, and the weak-entity filter is scoped as STRUCTURAL only with an explicit reason ('corpus-specific stopword lists are the consuming app's concern, not a general-purpose library's') — a clean library-vs-application boundary rule. Caveat: the second detector in reflection.ts honours none of this (see antipattern 1).

findings.title: Namespaced reason prefixes as the audit filter, with the predicate exported to consumers
findings.whatItIs: Soft-delete reasons follow a prefix convention: no prefix = real lifecycle event, `user:` = explicit human action, `system:` = automated platform action (visible but filterable), `preview:` = speculative/rolled-back UX (HIDDEN by default). shouldHideReason(reason, {hideReasonPrefixes, includeAll}) implements it, defaults to hiding `preview:`, and is exported 'so consumers can use the same filter against their own audit pipelines'. It is documented as convention-only, with the behaviour non-adopters get named explicitly.
findings.whyItMatters: A zero-schema-change way to make a free-text audit reason machine-filterable, plus the right ergonomic call: ship the filter predicate so the library and its consumers cannot end up with two divergent classifiers. The honesty about it being unenforced is the part most such conventions omit.

findings.title: Time decay is opt-in because the field it keys on is never written by normal operation
findings.whatItIs: decayConfidence keys on lastAccessedAt, but nothing refreshes that field unless retrieval runs with recordAccess (off by default, because a write is not a side effect of a read). So decay measured age since creation, not disuse, and it compounds per pass. reflect() now takes {decay?: boolean}, defaults off, and gates on a strict `opts.decay === true`. decayConfidence stays exported for callers that mean it.
findings.quote: the shipped host reached this function every six hours through its contradiction scan, so a node older than a couple of months fell to the 0.1 floor within a day and was suppressed in retrieval. `generateAuditReport` reached it too, which made producing an audit mutate the data it audits.
findings.whyItMatters: A whole causal chain worth internalising before building recency decay anywhere: an access-decay policy is only meaningful if something records access; recording access on a read is itself a consequential design decision; and a compounding multiplier reached by a background scheduler collapses to its floor far faster than the per-pass rate suggests. The regression test pins it as four named properties, including 'twenty passes = five days at the host cadence cannot compound'.

findings.title: A structural marker is corroborating evidence of retirement, never a liveness switch
findings.whatItIs: Graphs written before metadata.retiredBy carry four producer-specific markers (deletedAt / forgottenAt / supersedes-edge-only / bare validUntil). isAdministrativelyRetired recovers all of them, but the supersedes-edge branch requires the node to ALSO carry a numeric validUntil — because `supersedes` is a public DirectedEdge type with no direction validation, and a caller-supplied edge would otherwise retire a live node markerlessly, clock-freely (invisible even to the retiredAt:0 audit hatch), persistently, and irreversibly (blocksReingest would read it as a supersede tomb). retiredAtOf provides a four-step fallback chain so retired() never sorts on undefined.
findings.quote: `supersededIds` is not optional in spirit ... This is the only site that DECIDES retirement and then MUTATES, so a legacy tomb it fails to recognise is not merely served, it is rewritten ... A v0.8.0-era graph stays repairable by a later release; one this function has downgraded does not.
findings.whyItMatters: The general rule — a structural artifact may corroborate a state but must never be sufficient to establish it when that artifact is caller-writable — plus the sharpest migration insight in the repo: the dangerous call sites are those that decide state AND mutate, because a misclassification there is not a bad read, it destroys the evidence a future release would need to repair the data. The test craft mirrors it: a golden .gai fixture holding one tomb per legacy producer, a read-path suite, and a SEPARATE write-path suite whose header explains why the read-path suite structurally cannot catch this class.

findings.title: Destructive paths are fenced by verification or explicit opt-in, and the fences carry measurements
findings.whatItIs: Three fences, one doctrine. (a) deduplicateGraph buckets by 32-bit DJB2 contentHash then SUB-GROUPS by exact content string and merges only within a content bucket, so a hash collision leaves both nodes standing. (b) It excludes retired nodes as both duplicate and canonical, because forget-then-restore deliberately produces two nodes with one hash and 'keep the first' is insertion order — it could destroy either the audit record or the live memory. (c) buildGraph calls pruneGraph with removeOrphans:false; the hard-delete capability survives but is documented as explicitly OUTSIDE the indelibility theorem.
findings.quote: A collision leaves both nodes standing, which is the correct failure direction: a redundant node costs space, a destroyed one costs a memory. ... Measured on the LongMemEval corpus that silently discarded 80 of 3,747 nodes at q=1 (2.1%) and 467 of 19,416 at q=5 (2.4%).
findings.whyItMatters: Three reusable moves: name the correct FAILURE DIRECTION for every destructive operation and design toward it; treat 'keep the first' as insertion-order nondeterminism silently choosing between semantically different survivors; and when a guarantee has an exception, scope the guarantee in writing (Theorem 1 covers canonical-layer writes; opt-in maintenance is outside it) rather than pretending the exception does not exist. They also kept a measurement showing the retained edge-pruning removes zero edges in practice.

findings.title: One slot per node id structurally cannot represent a merge conflict — three options, all wrong
findings.whatItIs: SPEC.md §8.1 states that merging two copies of a graph where both edited node n1 must yield a graph containing BOTH revisions marked in conflict, and that with one slot per id the implementation has exactly three choices, all wrong: overwrite one (silent loss), mint a fresh id for the loser (loses that these are two revisions of the same thing), or emit the conflict edge as the self-loop n1 -> n1 (asserts a fact conflicts with itself). The proposed v2 fix is (id, rev) identity with id stable across content changes — and explicitly NOT content-derived ids.
findings.quote: With one slot per id the implementation has three choices and all are wrong ... The `contradicts` edge type already exists; it has nowhere meaningful to point.
findings.whyItMatters: It is the load-bearing argument for why a revisioned node identity is required by any system promising indelibility plus multi-writer merge, and it exposes an honest tension in the shipped code: today's supersede IS option two (a fresh nanoid for the replacement), mitigated only by the supersedes edge. That works for single-writer append-only history and is exactly why merge is absent from v1. Anyone designing a mergeable knowledge store should decide (id, rev) before shipping v1, not after.

findings.title: Process: defect-archaeology comments, guard-neutralisation tests, changelog errata
findings.whatItIs: Three reinforcing conventions. (1) Nearly every guard carries the incident that motivated it, the measurement, what breaks if removed, and the alternative rejected and why — including one comment that explicitly refuses to copy a neighbouring guard's refusal as cargo cult and re-derives it on independent grounds.
