(2) Tests are framework-free tsx scripts with numbered claim headers and a local check(name, cond, detail); the confidence suite states every guard is written so removing it turns a NAMED check red, and one 'test' is a source scan asserting nothing under src/core/query/ can import the confidence writer. (3) The changelog analyses consumer impact (reader's view vs constructor's view of a type change) and carries an '### Errata (added after release)' section admitting an omission that silently broke a downstream classifier.
findings.quote: Every guard below is written so that removing the guard makes a named check go red — see the neutralisation log in the milestone report.
findings.whyItMatters: Hand-rolled mutation testing with an audit trail, and rationale stored next to the code it constrains, mean a future maintainer who deletes a guard learns from the failing check's NAME what invariant they broke. The errata convention (record the omission instead of quietly fixing it, then freeze the affected strings and name specific traps for future authors — 'do not introduce the word signature into any message') is a rare and genuinely honest release practice. The ROADMAP is likewise a triage policy whose default answer for borderline features is 'build it as a separate package'.

antipatterns.title: Two contradiction detectors with incompatible gates; the reflection one cannot fire on a real correction
antipatterns.why: reflection.detectContradictions requires jaccard(entities) > 0.6 AND cosine(tfidf) < 0.15 — high entity overlap plus LOW lexical similarity. A genuine textual correction is by construction lexically SIMILAR to what it corrects (same subject, same numbers, one negation), so the gate excludes the canonical case. The append-time detector in sdk/index.ts uses a completely different algorithm (>=2 strong shared entities, >=60 chars, a marker, no similarity term) and does flag it. Yet ROADMAP.md advertises reflect() contradictions as a core feature, and the audit report's 'Contradictions Detected' section is sourced exclusively from the reflection detector — so that section is plausibly always empty. reflection.ts also hardcodes a 50-word English GENERIC_TERMS list (including 'gaussian', 'linear', 'binary') — corpus-specific stopwords inside a general-purpose library, exactly what sdk/index.ts declares out of scope for the other detector.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/optimization/reflection.ts:128 (gate) vs src/sdk/index.ts:255 (gate); src/core/optimization/reflection.ts:359 (GENERIC_TERMS) vs src/sdk/index.ts:176; src/core/audit/audit-exporter.ts:256; ROADMAP.md:31. MEASURED against this checkout with bun on the README's own advertised example (README.md:219): the pair scores jaccard(entities)=0.833 and cosine(tfidf)=0.729 — passes >0.6 but fails <0.15. Append-time reported 1 contradiction; reflect() reported 0 across 4 consecutive calls. Two further hand-built pairs designed to trip the reflection gate also returned 0.

antipatterns.title: "Detection" mutates the graph, unboundedly, and generating an audit still mutates the data it audits
antipatterns.why: reflect() is presented as analysis but writes: detectContradictions inserts a `contradicts` edge per detection with NO existence check (unlike inferEdges, which maintains existingPairs, and discoverConnections, which checks alreadyConnected), and inferEdges inserts up to 100 transitive edges per call. generateAuditReport calls reflect() unconditionally, so producing an audit still mutates the edge set — the decay fix addressed only the confidence axis, and the regression test asserts only confidences, never directedEdges.size, so the remaining mutation is unpinned. On a host calling reflect() on a schedule (the decay comment says the shipped host did so every six hours), each detected pair would accrete a fresh duplicate contradicts edge forever.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/optimization/reflection.ts:141 (no existence check) vs src/core/optimization/reflection.ts:324 (inferEdges dedups) and src/core/optimization/reflection.ts:237 (discoverConnections dedups); src/core/audit/audit-exporter.ts:260; tests/unit/reflect-no-decay.test.ts:102 (D3 asserts confidence only)

antipatterns.title: Adjudication has nowhere to live, and reflection never consults retirement
antipatterns.why: Contradiction.resolved is set to false at both construction sites and read nowhere in the repo; contradictions are ephemeral values never persisted into the graph. The README promises the owner may 'supersede, keep both, or reject', but only supersede leaves a trace — 'keep both' and 'reject' are unrepresentable, so the same conflict is re-reported on every scan. Compounding it, reflection.ts imports nothing from retirement.ts: both detectContradictions and discoverConnections filter only on node.type and content length, so a superseded tomb keeps participating in contradiction detection against its own replacement (which by construction shares its entities and carries a correction marker) and in cross-domain discovery. Every other consumer in the repo — dedup, ingest, traversal, serialization, giki, enrichment — consults retirement; reflection is the hole.

antipatterns.title: Health metrics and entity reports conflate tombstones with weak live memories
antipatterns.why: generateHealthReport walks all nodes in one loop and, in the same pass, adds every node's confidence to totalConfidence and counts every node under 0.5 as lowConfidenceNodes — while separately counting the retired ones. Since retirement drives confidence to exactly 0, avgConfidence is dragged down in proportion to how much the owner has forgotten, and lowConfidenceNodes is weak_live + retired. That is precisely the conflation retirement.ts forbids ('Confidence is NOT a liveness signal in either direction'), reintroduced in the surface whose job is reporting on retirement, and both are printed as top-line health metrics next to the retired counts. Separately, EntityReport.facts carries no retired flag and generateEntityReports includes retired nodes, so the audit markdown's 'Top Entities' interleaves retired and live facts distinguishable only by a 0% confidence badge — while Graphnosis.retired() does the same job properly (node, reason, instant, deterministic sort with an id tie-break).

antipatterns.title: None of this territory reaches the AI-facing MCP surface, and MCP ingest drops contradictions
antipatterns.why: The MCP server registers exactly five tools: load_graph, ingest_files, update_graph, query, export. There is no supersede, deleteNode, setConfidence, retired, forgetTopic/previewForgetTopic, or audit tool — so for a library pitched as memory for AI harnesses, an agent can write and read memories but can never correct, weight, forget, or audit them. Worse, update_graph bypasses the SDK facade and calls addDocumentsToGraph directly, while detectNewContradictions lives only in the SDK wrapper (appendWithOptions), so contradictions are silently dropped on the one ingest path where an agent is most likely to be writing conflicting information.

antipatterns.title: The correction write path discards provenance, recomputes IDF per node, builds no association edges
antipatterns.why: applyAdd is the shared node minter for add/edit/supersede and hardcodes source: {file: 'human-correction', offset: 0}. So the replacement for a superseded fact no longer belongs to the document it corrects: per-source ingest dedup keys on chunkKey (file+type+order) and can never match or update it on a later sync, and cascadeSoftDelete's same-source sweep will not reach corrections when the source is forgotten — against the stated §1 Provenance requirement, the only lineage a correction carries is the supersedes edge. applyAdd also calls computeIdf on every single add, and importCorrections calls applyAdd once per chunk, making bulk import O(chunks x vocabulary). And a correction node gets at most one directed edge and joins the undirected association graph not at all, so in a dual-graph system the highest-confidence content is the least connected.

Related doc rot: AGENTS.md:41,43,55 and CLAUDE.md:68,135,140,142 still describe .aikg, always-on ~1%/day decay, orphan auto-pruning, and soft-delete at confidence 0.1 — all false in current code, so the agent-facing summaries are the least reliable documents in the repo while the accurate rationale lives only in source comments.

surveys.territory: agent/MCP tool surface, skills & authority ceiling
surveys.summary: This territory splits cleanly in two, and the split is the most important fact about it. The OSS MCP server in src/mcp/* is a thin, unremarkable 5-tool stdio/HTTP wrapper (~370 LOC: load_graph, ingest_files, update_graph, query, export) with real multi-tenancy and path-scoping defects. Almost all the intellectual product lives in two documents describing systems this repo does not implement: GRAPHNOSIS.md is the closed-source desktop app's agent instruction sheet (~48 tools in 10 groups, engram/cortex/.gnn/.gll vocabulary, version 1.13.0 vs package.json 0.11.0), and SPEC.md section 8 is an explicitly-labelled unimplemented format proposal carrying maxAutonomy, skill subgraphs and per-layer conformance. What is genuinely rare here is instruction design and format-level authority modelling: a tool taxonomy whose organizing axis deliberately switches from intent to determinism tier partway down, a query-transformation curriculum keyed to the retrieval engine's named blind spots, write privilege enforced by physical file separation rather than by a check, and an authority ceiling that is monotone under composition and fails closed on absence. The best actual code in scope is src/core/errors.ts, an error taxonomy explicitly engineered to survive JSON-RPC and bundler-duplicated module instances.

findings.title: Tool taxonomy switches axis on purpose: intent for 6 groups, determinism tier for 4
findings.whatItIs: 48 MCP tools are organized into 10 named groups. Groups 1-6 (Core memory, Engram discovery, Structured recall, Source operations, Engram operations, Skills/SOPs) are grouped by INTENT — what the agent is trying to do — because those tools always work. Groups 7-10 flip the axis to the guarantee the tool gives: 'Brain maintenance (5) — read-only windows into the background brain', 'Approximate (2) — similarity scans, no LLM', 'Conditional (1) — deterministic by default, LLM-aware when enabled', 'Non-deterministic (6) — require local LLM (Ollama) on the user's machine'. Two of the three tier headers ARE the tier name, so the determinism contract is unavoidable when reading the tool list rather than buried in a description. The single Conditional tool, `edit`, resolves its own ambiguity per call: its response carries a `mode` field reporting which path actually ran (deterministic / gnn-expanded / llm-assisted).
findings.quote: `edit` ... The `mode` field reports which path ran (`deterministic` / `gnn-expanded` / `llm-assisted`).
findings.whyItMatters: A tool whose determinism depends on host configuration is unusable by an agent that needs to know how much to trust the result. The standard answers are bad: splitting into three tools multiplies the surface; documenting 'may use an LLM' gives no per-call signal. Reporting the tier as a field on the response means the agent learns the tier of the actual call, not of the tool. The axis-switch is the second half: always-available tools should be picked by intent and conditionally-available tools by contract, and forcing both into one taxonomy loses information.

findings.title: "Two non-negotiable habits": instructions that pre-empt the model's own excuses inline
findings.whatItIs: The agent instruction file opens, before any tool list, with exactly two rules labelled non-negotiable: recall before answering, and remember proactively in the user's own words. Each carries an anti-rationalization clause aimed at a specific observed failure: 'even if your own history looks empty' (kills 'my context has nothing about X, therefore nothing exists'), 'Don't wait to be asked' (kills deference), 'Save in the user's language; never translate "for safekeeping"' (kills a helpful behaviour that silently breaks a lexical index, with the model's own rationalization scare-quoted back at it), and 'call `stats` if you don't know the engrams yet' (removes the 'I don't know where to put it' excuse by naming the tool). The highest-value operational rule — use `edit`, never a second `remember`, because a second `remember` creates a conflicting duplicate — is deliberately stated twice: once in the hygiene section and again inside the `edit` tool description, i.e. at the place the agent is reading when it would make the mistake.
findings.quote: call `recall`/`remind` **before** answering, even if your own history looks empty.
findings.whyItMatters: Most MCP instruction files are flat tool dumps and lose to the model's own reasoning about when a rule does not apply. The mechanism: state few rules, mark them non-negotiable, place them before the tool list, and close each predictable escape hatch with a clause written in the voice the model would use to justify skipping. The redundancy placement is separately transferable — repeat a rule at the call site where violating it is tempting, not only in the preamble.

findings.title: Query-transformation curriculum keyed to the retrieval engine's named blind spots
findings.whatItIs: A section titled 'Query well — recall quality lives or dies here' sits before the tool list and gives five transformation rules, each naming the engine property that motivates it rather than just stating the rule. Strip framing ('remind me', 'what did I say about' — in any language). Match the storage language, because 'the lexical index does not bridge languages', with a concrete heuristic (query in languages seen this session; if unknown, the current input language plus any other the user has used plus English) and a bounded retry policy ('Zero results -> retry in 1-2 other plausible languages before declaring nothing found'). Add 1-2 same-language synonyms, because 'TF-IDF has no semantic awareness'. Keep it dense: 3-8 content words, no stopwords, no punctuation, no sentences. Anchor on proper nouns with verbatim spelling and capitalisation and never transliterate. It closes with a worked cross-lingual example (Arabic user, French-stored memory).
findings.quote: Add 1–2 same-language synonyms ("locuit" won't match "trăit"; "live" won't match "reside"). TF-IDF has no semantic awareness.
findings.whyItMatters: The rarest artifact in the repo. Retrieval quality for an agent is dominated by query formulation, and virtually every MCP memory server ships tool descriptions instead of a query curriculum. Teaching the limitation ('TF-IDF has no semantic awareness') rather than the workaround ('add synonyms') is what lets the model generalize to cases the rules do not enumerate. The bounded retry ('1-2 other plausible languages') is the detail that makes it terminate instead of degenerating into 'try harder'. The engine facts backing it are real and documented in code — the SDK's own migrateAnalyzer records an incident where a 16-language stopword union silently dropped 'car', 'war' and 'die' from every English document at ingest.

findings.title: Escalation policy in the tool description, harness-aware pre-loading, in-band redirect hints
findings.whatItIs: The `recall` description carries an explicit escalation contract: 0-3 nodes returned, OR nodes that do not answer the question, requires calling `dig_deeper` with the same query BEFORE the agent is allowed to say 'nothing found' — a numeric trigger, a semantic trigger, and a forbidden utterance. The alias `remind` inherits the policy by explicit statement rather than implication. The description then adds a harness-level instruction: 'If your client uses deferred schema loading, pre-load `dig_deeper` before the first `recall`.' Separately, `dig_deeper` responses embed a control signal — a hint line reporting that the query entities also match source-file names, carrying sourceIds — and the instruction file teaches the agent to watch for it and stop to call `recall_source` on those IDs before composing an answer, because a whole document is relevant rather than a chunk.
findings.quote: If your client uses deferred schema loading, pre-load `dig_deeper` before the first `recall`.
findings.whyItMatters: Three transferable mechanisms. (1) An escalation rule expressed as a forbidden output ('may not say nothing found until X has run') is far harder for a model to rationalize around than 'consider escalating'. (2) The deferred-schema-loading instruction is the only case I have seen of an MCP instruction file reasoning about the host's tool-loading mechanics — exactly the ToolSearch pattern — and warming the escalation tool before the call that might need it. (3) Putting a control token in the tool RESULT gives adaptive multi-hop retrieval without a planner: the retrieval layer knows the match is document-level and says so in a token the agent has been taught to obey.

findings.title: Per-stage retrieval provenance with a >60% threshold that changes what the agent must SAY
findings.whatItIs: dig_deeper returns a three-stage labelled structure — standard recall subgraph, then a 'DIG_DEEPER — Source-filename expansion' section, then a 'DIG_DEEPER — Cross-engram entity hop' section annotated with the shared entities used — followed by italic provenance bullets giving node counts per stage ('Content match (recall): N nodes', 'Source-filename expansion: N nodes from M source(s)', 'Cross-engram entity hop: N nodes via M shared entities'). If the indirect stages produced more than 60% of the returned nodes, a warning is appended, and the instruction file binds a mandatory user-facing consequence to it: surface that the answer is mostly indirect expansion rather than a direct content match, and invite the user to rephrase.
findings.quote: If indirect stages dominated (>60% of nodes), a heads-up follows — when you see it, surface that the answer is mostly indirect expansion, not a direct content match, and invite the user to rephrase.
findings.whyItMatters: Almost every RAG system computes retrieval-quality signal and then discards it, or emits it as a score the model ignores. Two mechanisms fix that: the signal is a server-computed boolean (a threshold, not a number the model must interpret), and it is bound to a prescribed utterance so the consequence is behavioural rather than informational. The per-stage node counts additionally let a human debug WHY a bad answer was bad — content match vs filename expansion vs entity hop are three different failure modes with three different fixes.

findings.title: Layered .gai/.gnn/.gll memory: write privilege enforced by file separation
findings.whatItIs: Three physical files with different determinism contracts: .gai canonical (mutable only by the user via approved edit diffs), .gnn neural-network overlay (mutable by the GNN training pass), .gll local-LLM overlay (mutable by LLM inference loops). The guarantee is stated as structural rather than procedural: 'The LLM and the GNN cannot mutate .gai ... different files, different write privileges.' A capability table gives every optional LLM feature an explicit 'Writes to graph?' column, with edge prediction marked 'Writes to .gll, never to .gai'. Recall responses order the layers: attested KNOWLEDGE SUBGRAPH from .gai first, then CROSS-GRAPH CONNECTIONS (also attested), then an audit footer, then a fenced 'INFERRED LAYER (overlays — NOT attested memory)' whose rows carry six-character engine+kind+confidence tags [gll-assertion N%], [gll-edge N%], [gnn-edge N%]. Four agent rules govern it: cite as prediction not fact; attested wins on conflict (mention the discrepancy, offer edit); NEVER remember an inferred row; forget operates on .gai ids only and does not touch overlays.
findings.quote: Never `remember` an inferred row. That promotes a prediction to attested memory — the failure mode overlays exist to prevent. If the user confirms the inference, save the user's confirmation as a new attested memory.
findings.whyItMatters: The separation is enforced by the filesystem, not by a check that can be forgotten or bypassed — an overlay engine physically cannot write the canonical file. The subtler insight is that the whole scheme is defeated by one careless promotion, so the instruction names that failure mode explicitly AND supplies a correct escape hatch: re-save the user's confirmation, whose provenance is honestly the human, rather than the inference. The tagging convention (engine, kind, confidence, in six characters, on every row) is a cheap way to keep confidence-weighted content distinguishable inside a flat text block the model reads linearly.

findings.title: Sensitivity tiers with intent-scoped consent gating and a headless typed-phrase fallback
findings.whatItIs: Every engram is public, personal or sensitive. Recalls of public and personal engrams are silent; a sensitive recall triggers an in-app consent modal with four options (Allow / Deny / Allow-1h / Allow-today). Gating is scoped by intent rather than breadth: federated recall AUTO-EXCLUDES sensitive engrams the agent lacks consent for and never interrupts, while the modal fires only when the agent explicitly names a sensitive engram via only_engrams / target_engram. The agent-facing consequence is stated: 'Recalls may be partial — don't assume you can see everything stored.' For headless contexts (SSH / Docker / CI) with no UI to click, a fallback protocol makes the agent a strict courier: present the CONSENT REQUIRED notice verbatim, direct the user to Settings -> AI -> Consent Phrases, wait, then call confirm_data_access({phrase, tier}) with exactly what they typed — 'If they type SKIP, do not retry and do not invent the phrase.'
findings.quote: Federated recall auto-excludes sensitive engrams you lack consent for; the gate only fires when you explicitly name a sensitive engram via `only_engrams` / `target_engram`.
findings.whyItMatters: Three decisions worth stealing. (1) Broad queries silently narrow and only explicit requests prompt — consent fatigue is what kills consent UX, and gating on intent rather than blast radius is the right default. (2) Two of the four modal options are time-boxed, which is what makes 'Allow' survivable. (3) The headless protocol uses an out-of-band human-typed shared secret as the consent channel, with the agent explicitly forbidden from synthesizing it and a SKIP sentinel that terminates the retry loop. The agent-facing corollary — recalls may be partial, so do not report 'you never told me about X' — is the second-order consequence most consent designs forget to tell the model about.

findings.title: maxAutonomy: an authority ceiling that travels in the artifact, monotone and fail-closed
findings.whatItIs: A proposed optional node-metadata field maxAutonomy?: 'L0'|'L1'|'L2'|'L3' (L0 = never act unattended, L3 = may act unattended within the host's own policy) whose value is five normative rules, not the enum. (1) A ceiling is a maximum, never a grant — a host MUST NOT execute above it, MAY execute below it, MAY refuse entirely; the field can only lower authority. (2) It is monotone under composition: a subgraph's effective ceiling is the MINIMUM over its member nodes, so borrowing a skill can never raise the borrower's ceiling. (3) It survives transport, because it is node metadata riding the same serializeSubgraph envelope as the steps. (4) Absence is UNSPECIFIED, not unlimited — a conforming host MUST treat unspecified as the most restrictive level it supports. (5) A process minting or editing a node MUST NOT set maxAutonomy above the ceiling of the context it runs in. The spec states the honest limitation: advisory unless a conformance level mandates it.
findings.quote: Putting the ceiling in the file is what makes the guarantee survive transport ... what proposes an action does not approve its own limits.
findings.whyItMatters: The problem is real and undersolved: a portable skill or memory artifact moved to a different host arrives with its procedure intact and its constraints absent, and the receiving side has no way to discover it is missing something. Rules 2 and 4 together are the transferable core — min-over-members plus fail-closed-on-absence means an unknown, malformed or hostile artifact can only ever REDUCE the host's authority, never raise it. That monotonicity is what makes borrowing arbitrary third-party procedures tractable at all. Rule 5 is the format-level restatement of 'the thing proposing an action does not approve its own limits'. Note this is SPEC.md section 8, explicitly labelled PROPOSAL with nothing implemented — a design to port, not code to copy.

findings.title: Per-layer conformance L1/L2/L3, with the argument that ranking is not conformance
findings.whatItIs: Conformance is declared per layer with a stated reason: a file format benefits from many independent implementations because that is what proves the bytes are unambiguous, whereas a retrieval engine does not — ranking is a design position, and two engines that rank differently are not two implementations of one thing. L1 covers byte layout, header and integrity (frame, checksum-verify, reject). L2 covers the node/edge model and (id, rev) identity (round-trip every node, edge, revision and metadata field without loss) AND must honour the fail-closed unspecified-ceiling rule. L3 covers traversal, maxAutonomy in full and skill execution, and must enforce maxAutonomy as a hard gate. The spec explicitly declares that 'declaring L2 is a complete claim, not a partial one', and that an implementation declaring L3 while ignoring maxAutonomy is non-conforming — 'without that, section 8.2 is advisory text'.
findings.quote: A file format benefits from many independent implementations: that is what proves the bytes are unambiguous. A retrieval engine does not — ranking is a design position, and two engines that rank differently are not two implementations of one thing.
findings.whyItMatters: Two mechanisms. First, refusing to make ranking part of conformance is the correct and unusual call — it lets a format have real second implementations without forcing them to reproduce a scoring function nobody can specify. Second, 'declaring L2 is a complete claim, not a partial one' removes the social pressure to over-claim that ruins most levelled-conformance schemes. The sharpest detail is the cross-layer obligation: L2 must honour the unspecified-is-restrictive rule even though L2 does not enforce ceilings, so the fail-closed default is pushed BELOW the level that implements the feature and a merely-model-conforming reader cannot accidentally treat an unspecified ceiling as unlimited.

findings.title: Skills as ordinary nodes/edges tagged via `evidence`, with unbounded loops invalid
findings.whatItIs: A skill is a connected subgraph of ordinary nodes joined by ordinary `precedes` directed edges, distinguished only by the edge's `evidence` string: skill:seq for sequence (chain order is step order), skill:loop;max=N for a bounded loop, skill:branch;when=<predicate> for a branch, skill:call;target=<id> for a sub-skill call. The subgraph's contract (trigger, prerequisites, produces, success criterion, out-of-scope) lives in node metadata on the head step, and its authority ceiling is the minimum maxAutonomy over its steps. A loop without a bound is invalid. An L3 implementation MUST refuse to execute a skill whose loop edges lack bounds and MUST apply the min-ceiling rule before executing any step; L1 and L2 implementations need no skill support at all and round-trip skills correctly by round-tripping nodes and edges. Authoring and training are explicitly out of format scope — 'an implementation can be fully conforming without being able to train anything'.
findings.quote: A loop without a bound is invalid — an unbounded loop in a borrowable artifact is an unbounded obligation.
findings.whyItMatters: Representing procedures as a tagged pattern over an existing node/edge model rather than a new node kind buys three things at once: zero format change for readers who do not care about skills, skills inheriting every property of memories for free (provenance, retirement, supersession, signing, authority ceilings), and one query engine that retrieves both facts and procedures. The bounded-loop rule is the load-bearing safety property and its justification generalizes far past this format — any artifact you can borrow and execute must carry its own termination bound, because the borrower cannot infer one. Note the shipped app has five evidence types (adds skill:ctx, uses skill:calls) while the spec normalizes to four; the spec is the tidied version.

findings.title: Paired explain/execute skill tools and a resumable SkillExecutionPlan IR
findings.whatItIs: Two tools perform the same graph walk and differ only in output shape, with the choice bound to intent: walk_skill returns narrative SOP text with loop / branch / sub-skill glyph annotations and is for EXPLAINING to the user; walk_skill_structured returns a SkillExecutionPlan JSON and is the preferred tool for any procedural execution. The plan carries requires (plus requiresTypes inline type hints), produces, ordered steps[].calls with args and a captureAs variable binding, steps[].parallel for concurrent sub-skills, steps[].maxIterations surfacing the format-level loop bound, targetGraphId flags on cross-engram calls, and failureHandlers. A six-step agent protocol accompanies it: confirm every requires input with the user, check constraints.prerequisites and abort if unsatisfied, walk steps resolving args from prior captures, recurse into sub-skills, route exceptions to failureHandlers[0] instead of stopping, and report captured variables explicitly. Runs are resumable across sessions via save_skill_run (returns a runId, 'call as you walk') and resume_skill_run (returns captured vars, last completed step, and nextStepIndex). An unresolvedCall on a step must be surfaced to the user and never auto-created.
findings.quote: Two paired tools, two distinct purposes.
findings.whyItMatters: The pairing is the design decision: rather than one tool with a `format` parameter the model will get wrong, two names bound to two intents, with the preference stated ('Prefer this for any procedural execution task'). The plan shape is a compact and fairly complete agent-execution IR — named captures, declared inputs with type hints, declared outputs, parallel members, per-loop iteration caps, and failure routing — and the resumption pair means a long procedure survives a context reset without re-running side effects, which is the failure mode that makes multi-session agent procedures unusable today. The refusal to auto-create an unresolved sub-skill is the right call: a dangling reference is reported, never papered over.

findings.title: Error taxonomy keyed on caller action, built to survive JSON-RPC and bundler duplication
findings.whatItIs: Errors carry a stable string `code` plus a `codeClass` whose four values are actions, not categories: 'corruption' (quarantine, try a backup), 'version-skew' (NEVER quarantine — the file is fine, the reader is old), 'caller' (retrying unchanged will not help), 'config'. One Object.freeze'd map is the sole code-to-class relationship, 'deliberately the only place this relationship is written down — a second copy is how the app ended up with two divergent classifiers that disagreed with each other'. Message strings are frozen and codes are additive, with two named traps recorded in-source (never introduce the word 'signature' into a message; never change the 'Invalid .gai' / 'Invalid graph' prefixes) because a shipped consumer substring-matches them. Crucially it is a SINGLE class with a code field rather than one subclass per failure, because instanceof does not survive duplicated module instances or an esbuild bundle that inlines the package — 'the app's MCP bundle does exactly that' — whereas a string code does, and also survives JSON.stringify across an IPC or JSON-RPC boundary. Consumer API is three predicates: isCorruption / isVersionSkew / isCallerError.
findings.quote: `instanceof` does not survive duplicated module instances (two copies of the package in a dependency tree, or an esbuild bundle that inlines it — the app's MCP bundle does exactly that), whereas a string code does. It also survives `JSON.stringify` across an IPC or JSON-RPC boundary.
findings.whyItMatters: Directly portable and directly relevant to any MCP or IPC surface. Three separable insights. (1) The classification axis should be the action the consumer takes, not the internal failure name — and separating version-skew from corruption is load-bearing, because a prefix-matching consumer would otherwise quarantine a perfectly good file written by a newer version. (2) instanceof is the wrong discriminator at any serialization or bundling boundary; a string code on one class is right. (3) The incident that caused it is written into the source file, including the exact substring-matching snippet that broke and why, plus a rule that new codes are additive and messages are frozen. The follow-up defect is recorded too: the taxonomy shipped unreachable because the package exports map blocked deep imports — 'An unreachable API is an unshipped one'.

findings.title: No-egress invariant at the definition site, with a carve-out and a falsification procedure
findings.whatItIs: The SDK barrel opens with four numbered SECURITY INVARIANTS and names the enforcement mechanism in the heading — 'enforced by what we re-export, not by runtime checks'. Invariant 1 (the default path performs zero network I/O) names the two forbidden modules explicitly (core/enrichment/* and core/query/answer.ts) and the prohibition is repeated 1500 lines later at the re-export block, where the mistake would actually be made. Invariant 4 is an explicit EMBEDDING CARVE-OUT enumerating the exact seven symbols that DO reach the network, plus the trap that the plain sync append*() methods do NOT update the embedding index. The enterprise doc converts this into a three-step, five-minute auditor procedure: read the barrel's re-export list and the banner's exclusions; grep the transitive import graph for @ai-sdk/openai, openai, fetch(, node:http, https.request and find zero hits; run the SDK under `unshare -n` or a deny-all egress policy and confirm every operation still works. A parallel checklist covers embedding egress via adapter-id inspection.
findings.quote: Run the SDK behind a network sandbox that blocks all egress (`unshare -n`, a restrictive seccomp profile, or a deny-all egress network policy in your pod). All SDK operations continue to work.
findings.whyItMatters: A better format for a security claim than any threat-model document: the invariant lives at the definition site where it can be violated, the exclusions are named rather than described, the exceptions are enumerated as a closed list of symbols, and the whole claim is falsifiable in five minutes by a third party with no knowledge of the codebase. The step-3 sandbox test is what turns a promise into a property. The same rule is defended at the process level too — CONTRIBUTING.md's 'What we will NOT accept' list rejects any change requiring network egress from the core SDK — so it holds in code, in docs, and in review policy.

findings.title: log-redact: stable FNV-1a pseudonymization, because library logs are the consumer's data
findings.whatItIs: A 36-line module whose header states the whole threat model: when the SDK is embedded in a consumer app, its console.error / console.warn lines flow into the CONSUMER's stderr — dev terminals, crash reports, OS log aggregators — and anything sensitive that lands there is out of the SDK's control afterwards. Node ids are stable per cortex and cross-referenceable; source paths can name private folders. redactId hashes them with FNV-1a 32-bit via Math.imul into an 8-hex-char token, returning a ZERO_HASH constant for null/empty/undefined so the call is total. The stated property is that the same id yields the same token across calls, so one failing operation stays traceable across multiple log lines, while the original is unrecoverable. The header is explicit that this is 'cryptographically weak by design ... privacy hygiene in OUR logs, not authentication'.
findings.quote: Cryptographically weak by design — FNV-1a 32-bit. The point is privacy hygiene in OUR logs, not authentication.
findings.whyItMatters: Two ideas worth carrying. First, most libraries never reason about the fact that their log output becomes the consumer's retained data — a library that logs a node id or a filesystem path has exported it into someone else's log aggregator. Second, stable pseudonymity strictly beats redaction: '[REDACTED]' destroys the ability to correlate two log lines from one failing operation, while a stable hash preserves it, which is what keeps the logs useful for debugging. The honesty about the weakness matters too — unsalted FNV-1a over a known id space is brute-forceable, which is exactly why the header scopes the claim to hygiene rather than security.

antipatterns.title: GRAPHNOSIS_MCP_ROOT is set by the CLI and read by nothing — a sandbox that does not exist
antipatterns.why: `npx graphnosis mcp ./notes` reads as scoping the server to a folder, and does not. Every filesystem-touching MCP tool resolves whatever absolute or ~-relative path the model supplies, via four independent copies of the same 4-line expandPath helper with no shared root check — which is how the check got lost. export and update_graph will WRITE a .gai (mode 0o600, atomic rename) to any path the model names. The SDK's own security invariant #3 says 'Do NOT pass user-controlled strings; canonicalize before calling', and the MCP layer, whose path arguments are by construction model-controlled, does not. A single shared resolveWithinRoot(root, p) would fix it.
antipatterns.evidence: src/cli/index.ts:493 sets the env var; grep -rn GRAPHNOSIS_MCP_ROOT src/ dist/ returns only that line and its compiled twin. Four copies of the unchecked helper: src/mcp/tools/load_graph.ts:51, src/mcp/tools/ingest_files.ts:97, src/mcp/tools/update_graph.ts:109, src/mcp/tools/export.ts:41. Contradicted invariant at src/sdk/index.ts:16.

antipatterns.title: HTTP mode: one shared transport over one global session map means cross-client reads and writes
antipatterns.why: startHttp() constructs a single StreamableHTTPServerTransport at startup and routes every request from every client through it, over a module-global Map of sessions. getDefaultSession() returns the most recently created session process-wide, and graphId is OPTIONAL on query, update_graph and export with the documented default 'omit to use the most-recently loaded graph'. So client A's query with no graphId reads whatever client B just loaded — and update_graph/export make it a cross-client write. The enterprise doc's mitigation (put it behind a gateway for auth) cannot fix session bleed inside the process. Two further defects in the same 44-line file: sessions are never evicted (no TTL, no LRU, no delete — the SDK's own dispose() exists for exactly this and is unused), and server.connect(transport) runs after app.listen(), so a request arriving in that window hits an unconnected transport.
antipatterns.evidence: src/mcp/server.ts:141 (single transport), src/mcp/server.ts:145 (app.all routes all clients to it), src/mcp/server.ts:129 vs 150 (connect after listen), src/mcp/graph-session.ts:8 (module-global map), src/mcp/graph-session.ts:21 (getDefaultSession returns last inserted), src/mcp/tools/query.ts:7 (graphId optional), enterprise/enterprise.md:223 (no auth, use a gateway), src/sdk/index.ts:1412 (unused dispose).

antipatterns.title: GRAPHNOSIS.md documents ~48 tools this repository does not implement, with no header saying so
antipatterns.why: The root-level agent instruction file declares v1.13.0 and describes recall/remember/dig_deeper/edit/forget, engrams, cortex vitality, .gnn and .gll overlays, and 12 skill tools. package.json is 0.11.0 and the MCP server registers exactly five tools, none of which appear in that document. It is the closed-source desktop app's instruction sheet checked into the Apache-2.0 engine repo; the only disclosure is an oblique aside 500 lines into the README. Consequences: an engineer mining this repo for 'the MCP surface' specs against something that is not here; an agent handed this repo plus this file calls tools that do not exist; and the headline .gai/.gnn/.gll write-privilege guarantee is unverifiable from this codebase, since no .gnn or .gll reader or writer exists in src/.
antipatterns.evidence: GRAPHNOSIS.md:3 ('v1.13.0') vs package.json version 0.11.0; the five registrations at src/mcp/server.ts:38, :56, :74, :92, :110; the guarantee at GRAPHNOSIS.md:236; the oblique disclosure at README.md:512.

antipatterns.title: MCP tools throw bare Error with prose — the exact boundary the coded taxonomy was built for
antipatterns.why: Every failure the MCP layer can produce is `throw new Error('...')` with no code: 'No graph loaded. Call load_graph or ingest_files first.' in three tools, and 'File not found: <absPath>' in load_graph. Meanwhile src/core/errors.ts exists precisely because instanceof fails across bundled or duplicated modules and JSON-RPC, and its comment names the MCP bundle as the motivating case. A client therefore receives prose over JSON-RPC and is pushed straight back to substring matching — the failure the taxonomy was written to end. The load_graph message additionally echoes a fully-resolved host filesystem path back into the model's context, which is the same class of identifier the same package hashes before logging.

antipatterns.title: redactId is compiled and shipped but unreachable by consumers — the repo's own documented mistake
antipatterns.why: log-redact.ts lives under src/sdk/, compiles into dist/sdk/, and is not re-exported from the SDK barrel (zero occurrences of 'redact' in that 1626-line file). The package exports map publishes only '.', the two adapters and package.json, so Node's resolver blocks a deep import. This is character-for-character the defect the barrel itself documents and fixed for the error taxonomy, ending 'An unreachable API is an unshipped one' — and the same mistake sits one module over. A consumer who wants the SDK's own privacy-hygiene helper for their own logs cannot have it.

antipatterns.title: buildGraphPrompt injects English-only benchmark rubric into every consumer's system prompt
antipatterns.why: Two English regexes classify the question as 'preference' or 'aggregation' and prepend LongMemEval-shaped procedure text — including corpus-specific adjudication such as "'cuisine' = a national/regional cooking tradition, NOT a diet like 'vegan'" and instructions about claims: lines and src:User (turn N) tags. A caller who writes g.prompt(q) gets no parameter, no log line and no return value telling them ~400 tokens of benchmark rubric were prepended. It is English-only in a library whose own agent instructions make multilingual usage a headline concern. And it violates the library's own stated boundary: the contradiction-entity filter comment says corpus-specific word lists are 'the consuming app's concern, not a general-purpose library's'. The ctx.questionType router hook is the intended escape, but the FALLBACK — what every untagged caller gets — is the benchmark path, kept 'for exact A/B comparability'.

surveys.summary: This territory is a funnel: seven parsers (markdown, HTML, CSV/JSON, PDF, image EXIF, video container, conversation) plus five example fetchers all normalize to one `ParsedDocument {title, sections[], sourceFile, metadata}` shape, which a single chunker turns into `ExtractedChunk[]` carrying a parent-id tree, regex-extracted entities, a regex-classified node type (definition/event/data-point/claim/fact) and outbound links. Nothing downstream special-cases a source type — an EXIF GPS tag is rendered as an English sentence so it goes through the same chunker, entity extractor and TF-IDF index as a Wikipedia paragraph. There is a hard line between a deterministic zero-API core (parsers, chunker, entity extractor, identity extractor, edges) and four optional LLM passes (node enrichment, session summarization, query-time preference extraction, image vision), which are disk-cached on a versioned envelope keyed by prompt-version + inputs, write only into `node.metadata` (except session summaries, which add level-1 nodes), and are all gated by the same `isRetired` liveness predicate that gates prompts. The code is written as a postmortem archive: nearly every non-obvious branch carries the measured incident it prevents ("invented 95 of 211 identities", "80 of 3,747 nodes silently discarded", "evidence ORDER differed on 21/40"), and the test files are framework-free tsx scripts named after defect classes C1–C6. "Giki" is graph+wiki: LLM-free deterministic topic pages assembled from the chunk-time node types, every line carrying a `^[node:ID]^` citation.

findings.title: MIN_CHUNK_LENGTH exempts complete units: a length floor applies only to text that was split
findings.whatItIs: The chunker drops short pieces below MIN_CHUNK_LENGTH (20 chars) because splitting leaves prose fragments. But it first asks a structural question: `const isCompleteUnit = textChunks.length === 1` — if the section's content produced exactly one chunk, no split happened, so nothing was truncated and the floor must not apply. Short-but-whole units like a conversation turn reading "Paris.", "Blue" or "March 8" survive; a short leftover sitting beside siblings from the same section is still dropped. The failure it fixes is nasty: the answer disappeared while its section heading stayed, so the graph looked structurally intact and only the answer was gone.
findings.quote: A unit is complete when it is the only chunk its section produced: no split happened, so nothing was truncated.
findings.whyItMatters: Every chunker has a minimum-length filter and almost all of them apply it unconditionally, silently deleting short complete answers from Q&A, chat and tabular corpora. The fix costs one line and derives "was this truncated?" from the splitter's own output count rather than from any content heuristic.

findings.title: One canonical chunk identity: parentId must be the resolver's key or hierarchy silently vanishes
findings.whatItIs: `chunkKey(chunk) = `${source.file}:${type}:${order}`` is the ONLY key the graph builder resolves edge endpoints through, and the builder silently drops any edge whose endpoint key doesn't resolve. The chunker previously minted parent ids in a different synthetic shape (`doc:<file>`, `section:<file>:<title>`), so every `contains`/`precedes` edge was discarded, every child became structurally parentless, and the then-enabled orphan sweep hard-deleted them. Fix: the chunker computes `${doc.sourceFile}:document:0` and `${sourceFile}:section:${sectionOrder}` — the exact chunkKey shape — so producer and resolver share one identity function.
findings.quote: it previously used a separate synthetic shape (`doc:<file>`, `section:<file>:<title>`), which the resolver could never match, so EVERY hierarchy edge was silently discarded
findings.whyItMatters: Names the whole cascade — identity mismatch -> silent edge drop -> structural orphan -> node deletion -> content is unfindable and nothing reports it. Any key-remapping pipeline (chunk key -> node id, temp id -> db id) has this class of bug, and the general fix is that the producer must call the resolver's key function rather than reimplement its format.

findings.title: Entities may over-fire; identity extraction lets structural nodes corroborate, never originate
findings.whatItIs: `extractEntities` is deliberately generous (15+ script families, acronyms, camelCase, quoted/bracketed terms) because it feeds lexical retrieval. `extractIdentities` then runs over the built graph with a two-pass structural gate: nodes are sorted so content nodes come first, and a `document`/`section` node may only add mentions to a name the content pass already established (`if (structural && !entityMentions.has(normalized)) continue`). On the repo's own markdown the ungated heuristic invented 95 of 211 identities ("Governing Law", "Related Work") and not one real person; but dropping structural mentions entirely would have silently cost real people mention count, confidence and their knows/discussed-in edges.
findings.quote: structural nodes may not ORIGINATE an identity. They may still corroborate one that content has already established
findings.whyItMatters: The generalizable rule is that a signal source can be granted the right to CORROBORATE without the right to ORIGINATE — most systems only have a binary trust/exclude switch per source and both settings are wrong. Also a clean separation of concerns: over-generous lexical extraction and conservative entity resolution are two different jobs with opposite error costs, so they are two passes with different rules.

findings.title: Gate every content exit on one liveness predicate — ranking is not gating
findings.whatItIs: Forgotten/superseded nodes were excluded from prompts but still left the system by two other doors: LLM enrichment (which ships node content to OpenAI) and generated Giki pages (published output). Both merely ranked by confidence, which puts a retired node LAST rather than OUT — and last is inside a 200-node enrichment batch. Both now call the same `isRetired(node, now, supersededIds)` predicate that gates prompts. The Giki comment explicitly rejects the accidental-correctness argument: gating on confidence would have worked there by luck (retired nodes sit at 0, the page filters `relevance > 0`) and breaks the moment anything floors the multiplier or `edit()` resets confidence to 1.0.
findings.quote: Enrichment SENDS node content to an LLM. Forgotten content must not leave the machine any more than it may enter a prompt, and confidence ordering is not a gate
findings.whyItMatters: Deletion/forget features are usually implemented at the one exit the author was thinking about. This is the discipline that catches the rest: list every path by which stored content leaves (prompt, LLM enrichment, published page, export, log, telemetry) and route them all through one predicate. And the named anti-pattern — treating a ranking weight as a liveness signal — is the bug class this repo says bit it twice.

findings.title: Optional LLM passes: pure prompt-in/parse-out, metadata-only writes, prompt-version cache key
findings.whatItIs: The enrichment modules never perform I/O themselves — they export a pure prompt builder, a pure candidate selector, and a defensive parser (extract first `{...}`, JSON.parse, validate, return null on any throw), leaving the network call to the caller. `applyEnrichment` writes only `metadata.{synthesis,context,sourceQuality,enrichedAt}`, never content/contentHash/entities/edges, so hashes, dedup and retrieval scores are untouched. Results are cached to `data/cache/enrichment/{kind}-{hash}.json` inside a `CacheEnvelope {version, kind, hash, createdAt, payload}` — a `CACHE_VERSION` bump turns every old entry into a miss with no eviction pass. The cache key mixes an explicit `PROMPT_VERSION = 'v2-strict-cap3'` because of a recorded postmortem: without it the cache served stale permissive extractions and a 500-question re-run was a silent no-op. `temperature: 0` was added to cold misses with an explicit note that warm entries are deliberately NOT invalidated.
findings.quote: without a version field the cache served stale permissive extractions and the 500q re-run was a no-op
findings.whyItMatters: Three transferable rules: (1) the cache key must include everything that determines the output and the PROMPT is an input — otherwise a prompt change produces a clean-looking experiment that ran nothing; (2) a version field inside the envelope beats cache invalidation tooling; (3) keeping the LLM boundary as a pair of pure functions plus a caller-owned network call is what actually keeps a deterministic core deterministic. Also note `cacheOnly: true`, a dedicated flag so measurement runs cannot pay for or pollute the cache.

findings.title: Query-time preference extraction: category-gated, cap of 3, prefer zero over loose matches
findings.whatItIs: For recommendation-style questions the retrieval layer already finds the right session, but the preference signal is scattered across many small mentions, so the answer model over-generalizes or grounds in the assistant's own past recommendations. A pass runs ONLY when the router classifies the question as `single-session-preference`, calls gpt-4o-mini once per haystack session (lane-pooled, concurrency 6), and asks for AT MOST 3 self-contained user-voice statements with an enumerated disqualifier list (generic habits, past assistant suggestions even when the user engaged with them, world facts, question restatements, multilingual filler). The prompt says "If none qualify, return an empty list — this is the correct answer for most sessions." Output is rendered as a labeled `--- USER PREFERENCE STATEMENTS ---` block with `[session:|date:|turn:]` tags and prepended to the serialized subgraph so distilled evidence precedes raw turn evidence.
findings.quote: Return AT MOST 3 statements. Prefer zero over loose matches. A statement qualifies only if omitting it would make the recommendation worse or wrong.
findings.whyItMatters: Two ideas worth stealing: an extraction pass whose success criterion is "usually returns nothing", with disqualifiers enumerated as a list rather than implied by adjectives; and treating the VOICE of an extracted statement as first-class, because "the assistant recommended X last time" is the dominant false positive when mining preferences from transcripts. The cost model is in the header (~$0.75 per cold 500q run, near-zero warm) which is what makes an optional pass reviewable.

findings.title: Session summaries are level-1 nodes wired above the pruner floor and into the same TF-IDF index
findings.whatItIs: A ~50-session × ~50-turn haystack is ~2500 turn nodes; retrieval at 20-50 nodes cannot cover them. One LLM-generated summary per session becomes a real GraphNode: `type: 'session-summary'`, `level: 1` (above raw turns at 0), `confidence: 0.8` (deliberately below extracted content's 0.9), `source.file` = the session's own source so it stays attributable, entities capped at 20, and claims/dates stored as `' || '`-joined strings because the metadata value type is `Record<string, string|number>`. It is wired to every turn by a `summarizes` directed edge at weight 0.7, chosen because that exceeds the pruner's `minDirectedWeight` so the edges survive optimization, and it is added to the same TF-IDF index (IDF recomputed once after the whole batch) so seed-finding retrieves it lexically alongside turns.
findings.quote: Weight 0.7 > the pruner's minDirectedWeight so these edges survive optimization.
findings.whyItMatters: A summary is not a side table — it is a node at a distinct level with a distinct type, ranked slightly under primary evidence and reachable by one retrieval path, so "what happened in March" and "what exactly did I say" are served by the same query engine without displacing turn-level evidence. Picking an edge weight AGAINST a known downstream threshold and saying so in the comment is the kind of coupling that usually goes undocumented and later breaks.

findings.title: Multilingual by construction, plus prompts forbidding translation to protect lexical recall
findings.whatItIs: Every deterministic step assumes mixed-script input: one sentence-splitter regex covering nine terminator families (`. ! ? … 。！？ ؟؛ · ฯ ። ։ ।`), chunk classification patterns in ~13 languages per category, run-detectors for 15+ non-Latin scripts in the entity extractor, a ~250-entry multilingual capitalized-word stoplist (with an explicit note that German capitalizes all nouns), Unicode-aware person detection via `\p{Lu}\p{Ll}+`, role/organization patterns in 13 languages, and PDF section-header words in 12 languages. Both LLM prompts then explicitly forbid translation: keep 東京 not Tokyo, Müller not Mueller, București not Bucharest, write the summary in the transcript's language, but match semantically across languages.
findings.quote: Preserve entities in their original script (don't transliterate: keep "東京" not "Tokyo" ... keep "București" not "Bucharest")
findings.whyItMatters: The mechanical reason is the load-bearing insight: summaries and extracted claims are re-indexed into the SAME TF-IDF index as the original turns, so a summary that transliterated an entity produces a node that cannot be retrieved by the query that retrieves its own evidence. Translating at summarization time silently breaks lexical recall — a failure that no unit test would catch and that only shows up as degraded retrieval on non-English corpora.

findings.title: Ingest hardening: scan caps, bounded regex quantifiers, page caps, event-loop yields
findings.whatItIs: `extractLinks` caps the scan region at 256KB and bounds every quantifier (`[^\]]{1,500}`, `[^)\s]{1,2048}`) with the mechanism spelled out: an unbounded `[^\]]+` is O(n²) on runs of unbalanced brackets because at every `[` the engine rescans to end-of-string, and a few hundred KB of `"[[[[…"` froze the event loop for minutes; excluding whitespace from the URL class shrinks the backtracking surface further because real URLs have none. The PDF parser extracts in batches of 10 pages with `await new Promise(r => setImmediate(r))` between batches to keep the event loop responsive, capped at DEFAULT_MAX_PAGES = 2000 with an explicit `maxPages: Infinity` opt-out. The image parser switched from abandoned `exif-parser@0.1.x` to `exifr` specifically because it is actively maintained and fuzz-tested against malformed IFD structures. The incremental append validates the whole batch for conflicting chunk keys BEFORE writing a single node, so a rejected call leaves the graph untouched rather than half-mutated.
findings.quote: An unbounded `[^\]]+` / `[^)]+` makes the matcher O(n²) on long runs of unbalanced brackets (e.g. "[[[[…"): at every `[` the engine rescans to end-of-string for a closing `]`.
findings.whyItMatters: Directly portable hardening for any ingest surface: three distinct techniques (scan cap, bounded quantifiers with domain-justified limits, narrowed character class) in one 28-line function, each with the pathological input named. The batch-validate-before-write rule — "throwing mid-loop would leave the graph half-mutated, which is a worse failure than the orphan it replaces" — is a general transaction discipline for mutation passes without real transactions.

findings.title: PDF extraction joins glyphs by position-relative gap, then NFC-normalizes after the join
findings.whatItIs: pdfjs emits TextItems that in diacritic-heavy PDFs can be one item per glyph, so joining with ' ' shreds words and joining with '' merges them. `joinPdfItems` computes `gap = next.transform[4] - (item.transform[4] + item.width)` and `fontSize = Math.abs(item.transform[3]) || 10`, inserting a space only when `gap > fontSize * 0.2`, honoring `item.hasEOL` for newlines, and calling `.normalize('NFC')` on the FINAL joined string so combining sequences ('a' + U+0306) collapse to precomposed forms ('ă'). ~20 lines, no dependency beyond the pdfjs TextItem shape.
findings.quote: we compute the gap between consecutive items and only insert a space when it exceeds a fraction of the current font size
findings.whyItMatters: Two non-obvious insights worth the copy: inter-item spacing must be measured in font-size-relative units rather than absolute PDF units, and NFC must run AFTER the join because the combining marks arrive as separate text items so per-item normalization is a no-op. Nearly every naive pdfjs wrapper gets one or both wrong, which shows up as garbled non-English extraction. The dependency-selection comment (unpdf over pdf-parse@2/pdfreader/pdf2json/mupdf-js, with the specific structuredClone failure path named) is also a good model for recording a library choice.

findings.title: Non-prose sources rendered as prose at parse time; LLM strictly opt-in ($0 path)
findings.whatItIs: Image EXIF, video container metadata and CSV schemas are not emitted as key-value records — they are emitted as sentences inside normal `ParsedSection`s: "Image was taken at GPS coordinates: latitude 37.774900, longitude -122.419400. Altitude: 15.2m.", "Camera make: Canon. Camera model: …", "This dataset has 412 rows and 7 columns: a, b, c." Even the filename is mined into prose ("Image filename suggests: report q3 final."). Every parser is a "$0 path": metadata extraction is pure JS with no API calls, and the vision API is double-gated on `options.enableVision && process.env.OPENAI_API_KEY`, returning its own structured sections (Visual Description / Detected Objects / Text Content (OCR)) that are still just sections.
findings.whyItMatters: Zero downstream special-casing: one chunker, one entity extractor, one index, one retrieval path, and the LLM reads natural language instead of a serialized record. The cost is verbosity and some fabricated phrasing; the benefit is that adding a new source type is one parser file and nothing else in the system changes. The "$0 path" framing — the free deterministic tier always runs, the paid tier is opt-in and additive — makes the cost boundary explicit at the module level.

findings.title: Giki = graph + wiki: LLM-free topic pages typed by chunk-time node type, with node citations
findings.whatItIs: `generateGikiPage(graph, topic)` scores every node (entity match +0.5, content match +0.3, person-name match +0.8, enriched +0.1, then × confidence, retired excluded), takes the top 50, and partitions them BY NODE TYPE into a fixed page schema: definitions become the lead, `person` nodes become "Key People", `event` nodes are sorted by a year regex-extracted from their content into a "Timeline", then "Key Facts", "Data", and "Claims & Attributions" — the last preceded by "> *The following are attributed claims, not verified facts.*" with a visible confidence percentage per line. Every rendered line ends with `^[node:${node.id}]^` and the footer declares the citation format and the node/source counts. `generateGikiIndex` picks the top 30 entities by mention count plus every person node, capped at 40 pages, and emits a linking index page. Served as markdown download at `/api/graph/giki`.
findings.quote: *Node citations use ^[node:ID]^ format for traceability.*
findings.whyItMatters: The deterministic type classification done at CHUNK time is what makes a typed, sectioned wiki generatable with zero inference at RENDER time — the node type is the page schema, not decoration. And it is the counterweight to the deliberately-unreadable .gai binary: the same store serves an AI-native format and a human-auditable one, with citations that reverse the map. Distinguishing `claim` from `fact` in the UI, with an explicit "attributed, not verified" banner and a confidence percent, is honest epistemic surfacing that most RAG UIs skip.

findings.title: Example corpora selected for graph density, behind one fetcher contract and one registry
findings.whatItIs: Five corpora live as `src/examples/<name>/{config.ts,fetcher.ts}`, each exporting `fetchAll<X>(onProgress?: (current, total, title) => void): Promise<ParsedDocument[]>` and registered in a single `DATASETS` table that maps slug -> {name, fetcher, label}. Selection is stated in the config comments: 50 Wikipedia computing-history articles "selected for rich cross-references, dates, people, and concepts"; "~25 foundational papers that heavily cite each other" (abstracts only, "faster, no PDF parsing needed"); 31 curated Next.js MDX files; NASA rover photo metadata plus six hand-written mission-fact paragraphs; 10 Wikimedia Commons images (metadata only, "doesn't download full images"). The image corpus deliberately overlaps the others (ENIAC, Alan Turing, Mars) so cross-source shares-entity edges are demonstrable. Every fetcher is per-item failure tolerant (try/catch -> null, nulls omitted) and carries a documented per-source rate limit (Wikipedia 100ms, arXiv 3s, NASA 2s, Wikimedia 500ms, GitHub raw 200ms), repeated in AGENTS.md.
findings.quote: ~50 interconnected Wikipedia articles — Selected for rich cross-references, dates, people, and concepts
findings.whyItMatters: A demo corpus for a GRAPH product must be selected for edges, not volume, and this repo says so in the config file rather than discovering it later. The five corpora also happen to cover the parser matrix (native section trees, synthesized short sections, MDX needing pre-processing, live JSON API + curated prose, pure metadata records), so the example suite doubles as integration coverage. Corpus-specific pre-processing (stripping MDX imports and JSX) lives in the fetcher, keeping the shared markdown parser format-pure — a good boundary.

findings.title: Ingest-policy provenance per graph and per node, proven by a semantic parity test
findings.whatItIs: `CURRENT_INGEST_POLICY_ID = 'source-provenance-v1'` is written into `graph.metadata.ingestPolicyId` and into every source node's `metadata.ingestPolicyId`. Appending current-policy content to a graph built under an older/absent policy sets the graph marker to `'mixed'` and leaves legacy nodes absent-marked rather than retroactively relabelling them. The parity test between bulk `build()` and repeated `append()` opens by DEFINING the invariant as semantic and naming its exclusions ("Random node/edge ids, corpus-wide identity extraction, forward-only cross-document relationships, and exact undirected-edge equality are deliberately outside this assertion"), then compares sorted multisets of content fingerprints `[file, offset, section, type, content, chunkOrder]`, compares structural edges by endpoint fingerprint rather than id, asserts zero dangling endpoints, and asserts policy stamping survives a .gai round-trip. Sibling tests are framework-free tsx scripts named after defect classes (C1–C6, "six defects that all shared one symptom: content entered the system and quietly failed to be findable") with failure messages stating the consequence, and the determinism test asserts its own premise ("the two builds mint different node ids (fixture is doing its job)").
findings.quote: The invariant is semantic, not byte-identical ... Random node/edge ids, corpus-wide identity extraction ... are deliberately outside this assertion.
findings.whyItMatters: Two durable process moves. (1) Version the ingest SEMANTICS, not just the format, and stamp it at both container and record level so a mixed-vintage store is legible per record — the semantics genuinely changed (cross-source identical content used to collapse; now it stays attributable to both sources). (2) Writing down what an invariant EXCLUDES is what keeps it maintainable; without it the next person either weakens the assertion or chases nondeterminism that was never in scope. Naming tests after real defect classes rather than modules means a regression names the incident it revives.

antipatterns.title: isLikelyPerson makes every Title-Case phrase a human being, and the mention threshold is dead code
antipatterns.why: A "person" is any string of 2+ whitespace-separated words each matching ^\p{Lu}\p{Ll}+$. Combined with the multi-word capitalized-phrase entity rule (which does NOT consult COMMON_CAPITALIZED), the arXiv corpus mints "Attention Is All You Need", "Deep Residual Learning" and "Machine Learning" as person nodes with guessed role/organization attributes, knows edges to each other, and discussed-in edges to their sources. The two-pass structural gate fixed only the structural-node origination path; the content path is unguarded. Worse, the comment says "Create person nodes for entities mentioned at least once" and the code is `if (mentions.count < 1) continue` — count is >= 1 by construction, so there is no frequency threshold at all. The co-mention pass is then O(P²·M²) with array `.includes()` inside a double loop, so a title-heavy corpus makes false persons the dominant ingest cost.

antipatterns.title: 32-bit DJB2 used as the LLM enrichment cache key, in a repo that documents its collision profile
antipatterns.why: enrichment-cache.hashContent is a 32-bit DJB2 -> base36 hash, deliberately duplicated from the graph module. incremental.ts documents the exact same hash as "at cortex scale collisions stop being hypothetical — the birthday bound puts at least one collision at roughly 5% by 20k nodes and 25% by 50k". The session-summary cache is sized in its own header at ~25k sessions, squarely in that regime. A collision here does not error: it serves ANOTHER session's summary as this session's summary node, or another question's preference statements into this question's prompt, undetectably. The envelope already stores a `hash` field but readCache validates only `version` and `kind`, never the key material. Separately, CACHE_DIR is `process.cwd()/data/cache/enrichment` — a library whose cache location depends on the caller's working directory, with no size bound, TTL, or eviction over 25k JSON files.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/enrichment/enrichment-cache.ts:32 (DJB2), :16 (cwd-relative dir), :50 (readCache validates only version/kind), src/core/graph/incremental.ts:89 (the collision-profile comment), src/core/enrichment/session-summarizer.ts:11 (~25k sessions)

antipatterns.title: Message role is destroyed at parse time and string-sniffed back from a display label
antipatterns.why: conversationToDocument encodes role ONLY into a rendered section title: `${role === 'user' ? 'User' : 'Assistant'} (turn N)`. ParsedSection has no role field. Two separate downstream files then re-derive role by `s.title.startsWith('User')` — five duplicated lines in session-summarizer and preference-extractor. So the user-voice-vs-assistant-voice distinction, which the preference prompt spends a paragraph on, round-trips through a human-readable label; renaming it to lowercase reclassifies the entire corpus. The knock-on: inferUserProfile filters on `node.metadata.role !== 'user'`, and NOTHING in the codebase ever writes metadata.role (the chunker writes `{...inheritedMetadata, sectionTitle}`), so it always skips every node and returns an empty UserProfile — and it is an exported public API called from nowhere in src/ or tests/. Turn numbering `Math.floor(i/2)+1` also assumes strict alternation, so two consecutive user messages desynchronize every subsequent turn label that PreferenceStatement.turn cites back to the answer model.
antipatterns.evidence: src/core/ingestion/parsers/conversation-parser.ts:181, src/core/enrichment/session-summarizer.ts:200, src/core/enrichment/preference-extractor.ts:139, src/core/extraction/identity-extractor.ts:319 (reads metadata.role), src/core/extraction/chunker.ts:132 (writes no role)

antipatterns.title: parseRaw fabricates speaker attribution from paragraph index parity, and it is the universal fallback
antipatterns.why: `role: (i % 2 === 0 ? 'user' : 'assistant')` — speaker identity invented from whether a paragraph's index is even. detectFormat routes anything unrecognized here, and every structured parser (ChatGPT, Slack) falls back here inside its own catch, so a malformed export silently becomes a transcript with invented provenance. In a system whose entire premise is attributable, citable evidence — and whose preference extractor exists specifically to tell user voice from assistant voice — synthesizing provenance instead of recording 'unknown' is the wrong default. The tell that this is not trusted internally: the LongMemEval harness sets `format: 'raw'` on conversations whose roles it already knows, bypassing the parser entirely.

antipatterns.title: Giki: the topic argument is unused in Relationships, and index generation is O(pages x graph)
antipatterns.why: getTopicRelationships(graph, nodeIds, topic) never reads `topic`. It scans every directed edge in the graph, keeps any non-structural edge incident to a used node, and the caller slices to 15 — so the section is "an arbitrary 15 edges touching this page's nodes" while being presented to the reader as relationships about the topic. generateGikiIndex then calls generateGikiPage up to 40 times, and each call does a full node scan, a full edge scan, and its own collectSupersededIds (another full edge scan) — O(40*(N+E)) with three passes each, for a derivation that could be one pass. Within a page, citation de-duplication is applied only in the Key Facts branch via `usedNodeIds.includes(...)` (a linear scan inside a loop), so a person node matching the topic can be cited twice and the footer's "Generated from N graph nodes" double-counts.

antipatterns.title: An unimplemented feature writes a roadmap advertisement into the graph as retrievable knowledge
antipatterns.why: Setting `enableTranscription: true` on the video parser pushes a ParsedSection whose content is "Audio transcription via Whisper API is a planned feature. Currently, the framework is in place but requires ffmpeg ... Contribute at github.com/nehloo/Graphnosis." That section becomes a chunk, becomes a node, gets entity-extracted (Whisper, API, ffmpeg, the URL all match extractor rules), gets TF-IDF indexed, and can be returned as evidence in a query subgraph and serialized into an LLM prompt — indistinguishable from ingested content.
